subsubtopic: REQUESTED STUDY OF POST OFFICE SYSTEM BY HOUSE COMMITTEE-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a motion, under Standing Order 43, on a matter of extremely urgent and pressing necessity which I am sure will receive unanimous support from both sides of the House. In view of the vital importance of an efficient and reliable postal service to the economic well-being of Canada, and the apparent inability of the government to effect any significant change other than changing postmasters general, a process that only adds to the growing confusion indicated by lost mail, late and disrupted service bringing about the threat of a law suit, decline in house to house delivery, thereby reducing the number of letter carriers at a time of rising unemployment in Canada, continuing confrontationist labour-management relations, and all of this in the face of repeated illegal postal rate increases, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling):
That the government set up immediately a special parliamentary committee as recommended in the motion put before this House last May 18 to investigate all aspects of the Post Office system and bring in recommendations for urgent reform, and in particular to do this before the postal system collapses completely under the weight of its own incompetence.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 address my question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Media reports state that the United States government is disappointed at the National Energy Board's recommendation that a 56-inch, thin wall pipe be used for the mid-Yukon to mid-Alberta portion of the Alaska Highway gas pipeline. subsubtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL STANDARDS AND RESTRICTIONS STUDIES
speechtext: Are any studies in progress or contemplated into the effect on the competitiveness of domestic production versus foreign imports of environmental standards and restrictions in Canada?

speakeroldname: Mr. Mike Landers (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Environment)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Environment)
subsubtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL STANDARDS AND RESTRICTIONS STUDIES
speechtext:
As new environmental standards and regulations are developed, or existing ones reviewed, considerable attention is directed to the related economic impacts. In most cases decisions result from the work of joint industry-government task forces; a number of such initiatives are currently underway.
Because of the complex factors related to international competitiveness it has proven exceedingly difficult to isolate and quantify the impact of environmental measures. However, studies conducted in the U.S., Japan and in Canada concluded that such measures are relatively insignificant and non-inflationary. The OECD considers that environmental standards are not significant in international competitiveness.

Under the government's announced new program designed to promote a more thorough and systematic economic analysis of all major regulations which are primarily social in nature, social and economic analyses will be undertaken to assess the impact of DFE environmental regulations under development.

Canadian importers of eye drops and ophthalmic ointments are routinely requested to furnish evidence that these products have been manufactured under conditions that are identical to those required in Canada. subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have had a very interesting and intelligent debate. I hope I can follow the same track. Seriously, coming from the city of Calgary, which is the oil centre of Canada, I am very proud to take part in this debate today. I think I can restate carefully and correctly this party's policy with regard to this pipeline.
From questions put today by the opposition and answers given by the government, we believe that one of the ways to turn around the lagging economy of Canada is to get on with the building of this pipeline. Everyone is on all fours in that regard. However, we have been presented with a bill and an agreement which forms part of the bill. That needs to be examined. When we are passing a bill in parliament we want to do the right thing for the good of Canada, the good of the industry and, in particular, to start Canada back on the trail from the lagging economy which is being caused by the government's economic policies.
Northern Pipeline
By way of introduction, it is interesting to note that when we are dealing with pipelines we must deal with the whole ball of wax, the oil and gas industry. I have in my hand a copy of a report from the Canadian Petroleum Association which presented a brief some time ago and which I have incorporated into many speeches.
The western petroleum industry, exclusive of refining and marketing, currently spends, and has done so for ten years, approximately $1 billion per year. Over 85 per cent of that money is spent in Canada for goods, services, and payments to the government. Of the major expenditures made for oil and gas pipeline, gas plants, fittings, pressure vessels and pumps, over 80 per cent was spent in eastern Canada, a large part of it in the province of Quebec. The majority of its capital expenditures were made in Canada as a result of tariff protection.
Oil and gas revenues paid to the western provinces have directly, and this is the point I want to make first, benefited all Canadian taxpayers in savings to the federal government in federal-provincial equalization payments. In addition, the federal government is the major recipient of income taxes on the corporate profits of all companies directly or indirectly affected, not only the oil and gas industries but all the tertiary industries that supply the pipes, valves, Fixtures and other parts that make up the pipeline of which Canada has good experience building in the past.
I listened to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), whom I have known for a number of years, dealing with natural gas. He mentioned, and I endorse those figures, that we produced in western Canada five trillion cubic feet of gas in 1976 and five trillion cubic feet of gas in 1977. I remind the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands that most of that finding was in the province of Alberta at Suffolk where they drilled over 100 short gas wells and at Elsworth, which is close to Grande Prairie, where they have drilled some very large wells. In that area alone they have found two trillion cubic feet of gas. That is the proven reserves. The reserves in that area will rise to between seven and 15 trillion cubic feet of gas.
Alberta has a surplus of gas. We have heard a lot of pessimism from various speakers in the House that we are running out of energy. There are 3,000 gas wells shut down at the present time in the province of Alberta alone. Hundreds of millions of dollars were spent drilling those. In the Elsworth area alone we can produce one billion cubic feet a day, yet 3,000 of these wells are shut down at the present time. If there were a market at the present time-there is a demand in the United States-with a trade-off, that would net Canada in taxation $1 billion per year to the federal government and a half billion dollars to the provinces. This is all brought about by exploration and development.
As we know, this is a big risk industry. When the federal Liberal government brought in and implemented the white paper on taxation, exploration and development dried up. It was only after the scare of an energy shortage in this country that they listened to the Progressive Conservative party and

February 21, 1978
Northern Pipeline
changed the tax structure of the nation to encourage exploration and development.
You cannot expect exploration and development to take place if you take 100 per cent of the profits away from the corporate body which is taking the risk. You need to have corporations in this industry because it is big business. It costs a lot of money.

speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: I hear my friends to the left. They voted to shut down exploration. The reason I mentioned the development and exploration, as well as the great reserves now built up in Alberta, is because there is encouragement there. Compare the royalty system to the taxation system in Saskatchewan and you get the exploration where the action is, and that is in the province of Alberta.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: It has something to do with resources.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
If you are going to hunt partridge, you have to go in the grass and find them. You cannot stay in the house beside the fireplace. I do not want to get off track on this, but not very long ago some people were saying that there is no oil and no gas, that the pools have all been explored and developed. I have set those figures out to show what can be done on the basis of good economic policies, first in Alberta and now as suggested by my party in connection with exploration for gas and the development of this source of energy.
As to the bill itself, questions were put today by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) in relation to the approval given by the National Energy Board for the use of 56-inch pipe. I think everyone agrees with that decision because it gives us some assurance that the pipe will be made here in Canada, either in Hamilton or in Regina. It ensures that despite the lack of any guarantee there will be favourable opportunities in Canada. The United States does not favour a 56-inch pipe. The people there would prefer a high pressure pipe. If hon. members would look carefully at the agreement they would see that this decision may mean, as the hon. member for Yukon suggested in his questions, that the agreement will have to be renegotiated. That would be unfortunate, because, as a number of members have pointed out, it is already late in the day; the bill should have been before us very much earlier. Then again, questions were asked by my hon. friend from Hamilton West about the supply of valves and fittings, and we hear it would take about 18 months lead time if they are to be manufactured in our factories. This just cannot be done if we intend to move rapidly so as to improve our lagging economy.
As I say, it has been an intelligent debate, but before I get into committee matters may I say I was shocked when the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) lost his temper last night, with my hon. friend from Hamilton West particularly. He was irritated. I have a lot of quotations I could read but I do not want to take up time reading remarks

he has made against the Liberal party. But I would like to read something else into the record. Maybe a debate on a pipeline is not the time for poetry, but I thought the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands would like to be reminded of this poem-no doubt he is familiar with it. It is called "The Lost Leader". I think it fits the hon. member for Crowfoot very well. I shall not quote it all, and, by the way, I have changed one word. It reads:
Just for a handful of silver he left us,
Just for a ribbon to stick in his coat,
Found the one gift of which fortune bereft us,
Lost all the others she lets us devote .. .
One more wrong to man, one more insult to parliament Life's night begins, let him never come back to us!
Which means, night begins for him.
After the minister lost his temper yesterday I was reminded of the words of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he said "The path of glory leads but to the gravy." Well, they certainly led to gravy but they led also to an emotional disturbance last night, and I am glad Hansard did not put his swear words on record because even in Crowfoot it would have looked very bad for the hon. member who, I am sure, is in deep political trouble.
I want to deal with the judicial process set up to adjudicate disputes which are likely to arise from time to time, particularly in connection with clauses 14 and 15 which set aside any judicial review as to native claims, citizens' rights, disputes between contractor and contractor, employers and employees. I say this, and after I have dealt with the agencies which are to be set up, hon. members will understand why. I make the point right now that any process of judicial review is being taken away, the whole matter will be directly under the minister who will have power to authorize these agencies which are being set up to solve all disputes of the kind I have mentioned.
What does the bill provide in this regard? Well, there is to be an administrator described as the administrator of the agency. The administrator will be all-powerful. By "agency" is meant the northern pipeline agency, all of whose powers would be defined by order in council. The agency will be the complete master of the pipeline project, the biggest this country has seen since the building of the "national dream", the CPR.
All appointments are to be made by order in council. Under clause 5, the governor in council has the power to appoint the administrator. The administrator will exercise and perform all the duties and functions of a Czar minister. The minister who is chosen for the job, I do not know who he will be, will be appointed by order in council and he will be the minister responsible for the pipeline. If hon. members read clauses 14, 15 and 16 of this bill they will find that this special minister can be removed by the same process as that by which he was appointed. He can be appointed one day and removed the next to be replaced by another minister. And on the following day a third minister can replace him. Then, according to the rules of the House, should we in parliament see that something is going wrong with the project it might be impossible for us to address
February 21, 1978

questions to the minister who is responsible for what had occurred.
We have been promised 80 per cent of the content, but I still do not believe this figure will be achieved. It is a promise. There is no guarantee. There is no provision for control. There is only the hon. gentleman's word. I may say I have always accepted the word of the minister, but he is only one member of a government that is wishy-washy-

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: He may not be there.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
No. He may retire to a better climate, and I would not blame him. What I say is that we could try to clear up mistakes by putting questions to ministers but we would not be allowed to question a minister who had made the mistakes and who had been replaced. His successor would probably not talk to him. We have seen this happen with respect to the office of solicitor general. What we have before us is a very complex, autocratic approach to a question involving land claims, disputes between citizens, and other important issues affecting the public interest.
As I have said, we must have the pipeline. But surely we could be given a bill which would serve all Canadians better. We want this development because today there are one million unemployed in Canada, more unemployed than there were during the worst depression of the thirties. And no one, as far as I know, has suggested there is a world recession today although there is certainly a depression in Canada.
The minister to whom I have referred will be entitled, under this bill, to exercise all the powers of the National Energy Board. In other words, this agency would not only be all-powerful, exercising its functions by order in council without reference to parliament, but it would take over the powers and functions of the National Energy Board itself. The powers of the minister will be unlimited. It is he who gives direction to the agency. The agency dances to his tune. Moreover, as I say, the minister can be changed from day to day by order of the Privy Council. He can oversee all surveys, enforce the agreement between the United States and Canada, force land expropriations, and conclude land claims settlements, without any right of appeal.
Only on a question of law can there be an appeal to one judge of the Federal Appeal Court of Canada. What kind of nonsense is this? This is all hidden because everybody in Canada wants the pipeline and the employment it would generate to get the country moving again. Canadians are solid thinkers.
Calgary is a city of affluence because of two major industries, the gas and oil industry and the agricultural industry. Coming from Calgary and living in that environment I want to see this pipeline project developed. People in Calgary and Edmonton know better than people in any other city that jobs depend on the development of this project. However, they will think twice before they will give approval to this bill.
Northern Pipeline
We know what will happen in the committee. The Liberal government has a majority in the committee. The chairman is probably appointed by the cabinet, but he gets the nod from the majority of Liberals. The chairman of the committee will say, "Eldon, go ahead with your ten minutes of cross examination", or, "Move your amendment in ten minutes". This is a serious matter. In the committee a member can ask one question of the minister and the minister can talk nine and a half minutes, and that member's time is up.
Clause 14 of this bill grants to the governor in council the right to transfer to a minister-not specified-such of the powers, duties and function of any minister, department or agency and the right to exercise those powers and duties, and there is no right of appeal from the authority of the agency or the minister unless a question of law is involved. The minister can make law, rescind law, change law, legalize the illegal and make illegal the legal. That is the mess we are in.
Clause 15 merely restates that the all-powerful Liberal pipeline czar has the right to dictate to all concerned. Clause 15 states:
The Minister may, to facilitate the exercise of such of the powers and the carrying out of such of the duties and functions of a member of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada or any department or agency of the Government of Canada as are transferred to him, enter into an agreement,,. and carry out the duties and functions...
And be a czar. Clause 16 is even worse. That clause compounds the powers of the governor in council by decrees and edicts. There were no appeals from the decrees and edicts of the dictators in European history, and there is no appeal here either. Regulations can be made to modify any existing regulations under any act of parliament or under any act in reference to any person or corporation engaged in the development. What does that all mean? How can Canadians know the law if some unknown appointed minister, as the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands says, makes a decision and modifies the regulations? That is how the legal can become illegal and the illegal legalized. That is what those clauses say.
Clause 14 transfers power but does not give the courts a chance to review the situation. Orders in council can transfer powers from one minister to another. All that can be done without publicity and without any debate in parliament. It can be done by some unknown body, person or group. No dictator had greater powers.
We saw what happened when orders in council created a secret cartel in the uranium industry. Imagine what can be done with the powers granted in this bill! Everyone wants the pipeline, but we want a bill which will build the pipeline and serve Canadians while it is being built and after it has been built.
Clause 15 would allow the transfer of power from one minister to another. Power can be transferred from minister A to minister B, from minister B to minister C and so forth, without question. New agreements and orders can be made, and edicts and decrees can be enforced. Perhaps I should not say this in parliament, but where in hell is there protection of

February 21, 1978
Northern Pipeline
civil rights in this the biggest project since the national dream? Whatever happened to native land claims? What will happen to claims by other people from Alberta and British Columbia? What will happen to provincial rights? This law by order in council should be nicknamed the Liberal gas law. It gases the natives, the little citizen, corporations and public interests without giving any of them the right to survival with a gas mask.
We want accountability to parliament and to the country. We want accountability to natives and to all the citizens of Canada so that their interests can be protected. What accountability will there be if Canadian firms do not get the steel pipe contracts? What can parliament do about that? What can Canadian citizens, factories, and unions do about it? What happens if Canadians do not get the market for by-products? We heard the wishy-washy answer of the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen). He said he does not know, that it may take 18 months but that it is up to free enterprise to get geared up. I am sure he has much experience with regard to how long it takes to retool a factory, even in the automobile industry.
Let us be practical. If things go wrong and six months from now we ask these same questions-and God help us if this government is still here-will the answer be that there is provision in the bill, that it is the responsibility of the agency, or that things are done by orders in council which can be modified yesterday and varied tomorrow? Will that be the response if native claims are not settled or if Canadians do not get the jobs? We have no control over United States tariffs. How do we know that the Americans will not buy pipe from Japan?
On other projects the United States has used Japanese pipe. Will cheap Japanese pipe be dumped into the United States, and will the United States bid against our firms? The Deputy Prime Minister says we will have to compete. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce did not even know that Japanese pipe has been used to build pipelines in Canada. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands said he would have expected more intelligence from that minister. I have never expected any intelligence from him because I have known him for a long time. If inferior pipe and other inferior products are used, where can we go if there is not a question of law?
What happens if the cost of this pipeline escalates from $9 billion to $25 billion, as the national debt has escalated under this government in the last ten years? What recourse will this parliament have? What appeal will anyone have from decisions of the agency which is to be created as a puppet of the minister, who could change from day to day? How can we be sure of accountability? In my opinion there should be the right of appeal to a court of competent jurisdiction, the Federal Court of Canada, or a superior court of any province.
I am not talking about little disputes as to whether welders should go here or there. I am talking about substantial matters which go to the very meat of whether the pipe is manufactured in Canada or whether Canadian workers get jobs. All these tremendous powers granted to the minister will be bestowed by

order in council, and there will be no right of appeal except on a question of law, as set out in clauses 14, 15, 16 as well as in other clauses of the bill. Decrees and regulations must be monitored by parliament in a parliamentary committee from time to time. All orders should be tabled in the House so that Canadians will know the law from day to day, even as it is varied.
It was not long ago that the right hon. member for Prince Albert and Mr. St. Laurent made a deal that there would be the tabling of orders in council created by the Cabinet. The monitoring can be done by a strengthened Standing Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments, by the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works, or by a special committee set up for this purpose, that is, to act as a check and balance on so extensive a power assigned by law to parliament by this bill. We know the difficulties faced by the Standing Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments with respect to trying to get a reference out of the House as to orders in council. Every year thousands of laws are passed. Only a third of them were published last year. These safeguards must be spelled out in the bill. No other feathery citation would be adequate at committee stage.
In committee we will fight for a quarterly monitoring process which must be embodied in this bill. As wretched a bill as it is, and in that it lacks the necessary guarantees, the basic intention of building a pipeline to serve Canadian and American interests is present. It provides for Canadian interests to be involved and engaged in the building of the pipeline, the rolling of pipe, the manufacturing of fixtures, valves and all other necessary parts. That is what we will ask for in committee. If there is any delay in that regard it will be the government's fault and not the fault of this side of the House.
We have heard many promises, but there is no national energy policy, no northern energy policy, and no policy to settle native claims. The only appeal is to a federal appeal court sitting with one judge. On any other matter-and we are dealing with $9 billion-this court must sit with three judges. In this case, under this bill, one judge answers the questions. What is his power? He cannot vary the order of the agency. He can send it back with a direction. If the agency indicates that it does not go along with that, then it carries on in the same style and way, excercising its dictatorial powers over Canadians.
What protection do people have who own land? What protection is there for their way of life? The bill is polished like a red apple to create the biggest administrative dictatorial Liberal gang: the law makers, the law interpreters and, at the same time, emasculating the National Energy Board. Unless the National Energy Board is staffed with competent help- and it only expects to have 200 on the job-then even the slight influence the Board will have left cannot be put into action.

February 21, 1978

The hon. member for Yukon put it accurately and adequately. It needs repeating. He said the following:
Enormous powers will be granted under clauses 14, 15 and 16 of the bill. In the years of the Diefenbaker government, a gentleman's arrangement was made. The Deputy Prime Minister will remember this. Orders in council were to be tabled monthly and they were. Since 1963, that practice has been discontinued.
That was caused by the Liberal government. He continued: Unless you ask specifically for the tabling of an order in council, you never see it.
Even when it is requested, it must be pried out of the government.
He went on to say:
I request from the government, if not an embodiment in the legislation, at least an assurance that once a month copies of orders and decisions of the board and any orders in council made under this legislation will be tabled in this House. In that way we will be informed of the manner in which the regulatory agency is conducting this project.
I believe that under clause 35 of the bill the commission lands would be virtually wiped out. This cannot stand. As the hon. member for Yukon pointed out as an example, the pipeline could be built right through the town hall at Whitehorse and no one would have the right of appeal.
It is parliament that has and gives the power to delegate subordinate lawmaking by way of regulations and statutory instruments. It should remain there. This power is delegated by means of certain provisions of the legislation or acts it passes. To ensure that this delegated power is not misused, by the Statutory Instruments Act parliament established the Standing Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments. Section 2(l)(d) of the act applies to orders, rules and regulations of all kinds, with certain important exceptions that I will mention later.
The function of this committee is to act as a watchdog. This cannot be monitored under the bill. What watchdog do we have? We have no watchdog.
The second report of the committee reads as follows:
Parliament retains responsibility for the law of the land and to the extent that these detailed rules and regulations are not subject to parliamentary scrutiny, parliament is forfeiting its effective right to settle laws that must be obeyed by the people.
Parliamentary scrutiny of all such subordinate or delegated law is now an accepted part of the parliamentary tradition in the Commonwealth.
But that is not so in Canada. That is what the report indicated. If we ask for a committee to monitor this agency and the powers of the minister, surely that cannot be refused. Surely I, and other hon. members on this side, will be heard. We want this bill as badly as the government wants it. We will listen to reason in committee.
These skeletal provisions delegate excessive power to the minister. Also it is highly questionable whether the subdelegation to the extent allowed under clause 15 of this bill does not contravene the basic legal principle that a delegate may not subdelegate. Blanket delegation of this nature is only permissible, if at all, in emergency situations. If allowed to stand, parliamentary control would be difficult, as would review by the court. There is only review on the question of law. Likewise, it is a matter for serious consideration that the regula-
Northern Pipeline
tion-making powers conferred by this subdelegation would undoubtedly be very broad.
It is a vexed question whether parliament would or could review on a continuous basis, under the Statutory Instruments Act and therefore by a committee, the mass of documentation that would accumulate. The regulations pertaining to this documentation, as we see from clause 16(1) of the bill, may be made before the coming into force of the act. Perhaps they are prepared at this time, without us knowing anything about them. Surely those regulations should be laid before parliament prior to third reading in order for us to have the basic structure. With respect to this area, the bill hands over everything carte blanche to the executive. We are building a house with all the skeletal forms and parts of the rooftop, and at the same time allowing the government to put on the siding and do the interior decorating.
It is important to note, however, that even though the Statutory Instruments Act and the committe are intended as safeguards for the sovereignty of parliament, there is in the act an escape route by way of Section 27 which gives the governor in council the power to make regulations exempting the tabling of any regulation. If we ask for tabling, Section 27 can be invoked and the government can indicate that it does not have to table it. It is secret, like that secret order in council. Surely all hon. members want Canada to become an economically sound nation steeped in the protection of the law.
This is no time to play politics. We are all prone to put forward political ideas at times, but we have endeavoured to give the government some direction. Do not destroy the Bill of Rights, nor the works of the right hon. member for Prince Albert. The Bill of Rights indicates that all laws passed are subject to the interpretation of the Bill of Rights, which lays out some of the civil rights. I am talking about the rights of the native claimants. I am talking about the rights of any land owner, and I am talking about the rights in negotiating contracts between contractors and the government and employers and employees. The Bill of Rights is emasculated by this bill.
Now that I have dealt with the legal aspects of this legislation I want to lay down some philosophy. I have spoken in this House for ten years asking that we get on with this job and establish a special committee. I looked at some of the speeches I made when the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Sharp) was minister, in which I asked that a special committee be set up, but nothing was done at that time.
I would like to quote from "The Future of our Industry", a convention paper presented by J. C. Sproule at a meeting of the Canadian Oilfield Technical Society. He said, in dealing with the development of our resources:
It may or may not make good sense to leave undeveloped a country as rich in natural resources as the Canadian Arctic.	.
The population of the earth is expected to double in the next fifty years and to double again in the following fifty years. Fifty years is a relatively short time. Some of us can remember that long. Many of our children and grandchildren will be here at that time. Meanwhile, we must keep in mind that it was not the

February 21, 1978
Northern Pipeline
western democracies that are doubling population every fifty years, but is rather the over-populated "have not" countries who will soon be looking for living space. Our surplus living space would satisfy them. If we are not using it, or have not developed it, who has a better right to it than they?
In building this pipeline, in building the Dempster route, and in building the other pipeline and developing our resources, we will be protecting Canadian soil and resources for Canadians for all time to come. Of course we attract many immigrants to this country.
This is a very large project. This is the area it covers: from Watson Lake to the Alberta-B.C. border it is 440 miles; from the Alberta border to Caroline, from Caroline to the Saskatchewan border and from Caroline to the B.C. border, it is 806 miles; from southern B.C. to the U.S.A. border it is 105 miles; and from the Alberta-Saskatchewan border to the U.S.A. border it is 160 miles. On the Dempster route from Whitehorse to Watson Lake, B.C. it is 512 miles, making a total of 2,023 miles if the Dempster route is completed. So you see what lies before us.
Before concluding let me say that this is very important legislation. We are not going to debate it long because we want it to go to committee. We have asked for certain definite amendments to be made to the legislation to protect the native rights, the civil rights of Canadians, the rights of employers and employees in the signing and negotiating of contracts and, above all, the public interest, which takes in the cost of gas, if we are allowed to take that gas, something which we do not yet know, to the communities in the North, because it will be American gas that flows down there.
We are very fortunate to be so richly endowed with all forms of basic energy. History has proven that our industrial progress will be proportionate to our availability of energy. However, in recent years Canada has shown an international trade deficit in energy producing resources. As recently as 1950 we, as a nation, imported more than 60 per cent of all our fuel requirements, but in the 1970's we became self-sufficient.
We have oil and we will find a lot more. We have natural gas in surplus. We have one eighth of the world's supply of coal, and therefore we have energy. Our supplies of energy will determine the cost of energy and how we will conquer inflation. Let us get on with the job and go ahead with the project, but let us build in some safeguards because the people elected us as their members of parliament to guard their interests.

speakeroldname: Mr. Hugh A. Anderson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment
subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few minutes ago the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Wool-liams) mentioned that this legislation was important and that it was important for the Liberal party to have it passed. Let me point out in my opening remarks that it is not only important to the Liberal party; it is important to the people of Canada as well as to all the provincial premiers to have this legislation passed. A project of this size is important not only to one party. Surely it is important to the people of Canada as a whole.
May I say that the critics, mainly in the NDP, who argue that Canada should have obtained further guarantees of Canadian content before signing the pipeline agreement with the United States either fail to recognize that such demands would sabotage the whole deal, or else are dishonest with themselves, because there would have been no pipeline and no Canadian jobs, and this debate would not be going on at present, if Canada, in its negotiations with the U.S., had demanded guarantees of Canadian content. As the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) pointed out, they would have been buying a pig in a poke. I am sure the hon. member who is sitting on the NDP benches would not sign a contract not knowing what would be the cost involved.
There is no doubt in my mind that we would have had no pipeline to discuss in the House had we insisted that Canada obtain the majority of jobs on the pipeline and had we denied competitive bids on it. One cannot expect a rational person to sign a blank cheque to the Canadian people, especially in a situation where there is a cost factor which concerns us, that is, of course, the Dempster connection.
It would be hard to argue, if we were only talking about the Dempster connection, that there should be no competitive bids either on the pipe or on materials going into building it, but I suspect that the rationale behind the thinking of those eminent gentlemen who, as I mentioned, are mostly in the NDP, is that if it is American gas that will be going through the pipeline initially, then we should charge whatever the traffic will bear. I am rather amazed at this thinking because I assume that if we were in a similar situation I would not want our neighbours to adopt an attitude expressed in the words "to hell with the cost; the Canadians will have to pay it". I do not think that we, as good neighbours, should take such an attitude, especially when we have assurances from the companies that will be involved in the construction of this important project that they are competitive and that they are not afraid of the United States, of Japan or of West Germany.
Some members of the Conservative party also have expressed their fear, and yet last week we had a conference here in Ottawa at which the provincial premiers of the ten provinces met with the federal government and expressed the belief that the solution to our present economic problems lies in reliance upon the private sector of our economy. Yet day after day I read and hear in the House that we cannot compete with other countries. I wonder whether we have become a nation of mice, afraid to compete with our American neighbours.
This afternoon during the question period we heard remarks made by members of the official opposition regarding the Canadian dollar. Perhaps it is because I am from British Columbia, an export oriented province, that I think there is an opportunity with our devalued Canadian dollars, for us to export our products to world markets and thus pick up some of the trade lost over the years, perhaps due to foolishness on our part.
(Mr. Woolliams.]
February 21, 1978

I believe that opportunities exist if we choose to grab them, but I will certainly not stand up and say, "Poor us, we do not have the guts or the technology to compete in world markets."
I say we do, Mr. Speaker. We do not need guarantees that we must use steel at any price to ensure Canadian jobs. Those jobs will be filled by Canadians, but in competition, and not as a result of an arrangement that we sign a contract with the United States in case they compete against us. 1 do not accept that, and I do not think the people of Canada accept it.
There is an insidious movement in this country to belittle anything Canadian, whether it be this House of Commons or the ability of our companies to compete in world markets. It seems that we have a tremendous inferiority complex which is being encouraged by those who would like to change the system. That is something that I fear personally, and I will fight against it. Canadian companies have said time and time again that they do not need government intervention, that they can compete with the United States and other countries in the manufacture of pipe. The fact that we do not at the moment have companies manufacturing the fittings required is not a great drawback as they will not be needed for two or three years. It just means there will be opportunities for new companies in that area.
Perhaps I am parochial, Mr. Speaker. When the original discussions about a pipeline to transport gas from Alaska to the United States took place I thought that if we did not seize the opportunity to have this built on Canadian soil we, on the west coast, would find ourselves watching a procession of LNG tankers passing from Alaska to southern United States ports. I can assure this House that no one in British Columbia, and certainly none of the political parties in British Columbia, would support the proposition of increased tanker traffic off the west coast. We are all aware of the problems of oil spills in various parts of the world in recent years. British Columbians fear this because the west coast has the potential to be one of the world's greatest sources of protein as a result of the 200 mile limit on fisheries and because of the recently announced $150 million salmon enhancement program. We certainly do not want these resources destroyed.
Even if there were no aesthetic considerations regarding oil spillage off the beautiful west coast, there is a strong economic argument. We do not wish the blights that have occurred in other parts of the world to occur on our coast line. That is why, in August, I strongly supported the proposal for a pipeline.
This pipeline has tremendous prospects for western Canada-for British Columbia in particular and Canada in total, whether it be Quebec or Ontario that will supply many of the goods and services needed. There are tremendous opportunities for British Columbia since 700 or 800 miles of pipe will go through the province. We should use those opportunities well.
Some hon. members suggested that the GATT agreements would not affect a guarantee system and that we should not allow competition on the line. I was rather surprised that some
Northern Pipeline
members from British Columbia would suggest that we do not need to worry about the GATT agreements. With one quarter of our national wealth based upon export sales I fear it would be potentially dangerous for Canada to encourage the deterioration of the international trading system governed by GATT. There may be a loophole but, of course, if there is a loophole for us, there will be for other nations as well.
Coming from a province that is rich in resources I would hate to see our export market damaged because we were shortsighted enough to try to weasel into the GATT agreement a guarantee that was not written into it in the first place. I hope hon. members will look well ahead and not let us fall into a situation where we could be discriminated against in future through some legal flim-flam between nations.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the unreasonable terms proposed by the New Democratic Party would have doomed the pipeline agreement, and the charges of a sell-out which they raised would have been borne out. Such an approach would have sold out the $4 billion project at a time when most Canadians would agree stimulus is needed in our economy. I for one would not wish to go before the Canadian people in an election campaign and say that, in order to obtain guarantees, we lost the project, that it was a matter of judgment and our judgment was bad. I suspect the people would say that we did not have to worry about our judgment in the future because we would not be here.
If the Canadian companies which are vitally interested in this project say they can compete, why do we argue about it? Do politicians know better than businessmen whether they can compete? I think businessmen are able to take care of themselves and do not need the assistance of the New Democratic Party.
Opposition spokesmen have suggested irresponsibly that there will be no provisions to ensure that the 90 per cent Canadian input is achieved. The Canada-U.S. agreement asserts that the system will be built so as to "advance the national economic and energy interests and to maximize the related industrial benefit of each country." Legislation now before this House contains requirements about the input of Canadian labour, goods and services in the planning, purchasing and construction of the pipeline in this country.
The New Democratic Party is either unaware or has hidden under the rug the fact that the companies most vitally involved in supplying the pipeline project have not sought absolute guarantees or some assured preferential system for pipeline contracts. Mr. Speaker, the chairman of the steel company of Canada, Peter Gordon, says he is not only confident of Stelco's ability to meet United States competition for pipe in Canada but he indicates that the company may well compete with U.S. suppliers of pipe for contracts on their home ground. To build in guarantees would be to deprive Stelco of the opportunity to compete in the United States.
I wonder if we have lost our senses completely, Mr. Speaker. Just a week ago a conference suggested that the private sector of our economy is our salvation in terms of employment and prosperity, yet time and time again people who supposedly

February 21, 1978
Northern Pipeline
support that argument suggest that we should interfere a little bit here and a little bit there. I am probably the last of the free enterprisers, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member who spoke before me wants guarantees. He will give the most eloquent speech on free enterprise and government decontrol of the system, and then in the next breath say that these companies should come to parliament every three months and ask, "Am I doing all right?" It is ridiculous, and you know it is ridiculous. Be honest for once.
The New Democratic Party, Mr. Speaker, indicates that Foothills is apparently not competent either, although Foothills has said Canadian content in the pipeline will be 90 per cent. They have constructed pipelines in the west on numerous occasions and have been be able to fulfil the 90 per cent Canadian content. I still hear the "boo birds" say, "My goodness, we must do something to help those poor companies because we know the pipeline companies are telling us fairy stories. They cannot do it, the government must put in a guarantee".
We come back to the same thing, the government must do this and it must do that. We cannot take the word of a company which has been in operation a number of years and which possesses more experience than I have or any other member in this House has. Time and time again speakers on the other side keep bringing this point up as to guarantees of content, guarantees of this and that. I have more faith in Foothills obviously than they do. I have faith also in Westcoast Transmission which has had experience constructing pipelines in British Columbia.
The group of companies recognize, and we in the government agree, that over the past 20 years Canada has developed a number of large and highly efficient firms with the capacity to handle a project of the northern pipeline size. Two of the major companies involved in Foothills, Alberta Gas Trunk Line and Westcoast Transmission, have reported that their own construction in recent years has approached 90 per cent Canadian content. I accept their word. If other hon. members have information which I do not possess that these companies are unable to fulfil these requirements, we would like to know. I have heard no contradiction of the Foothills or Westcoast Transmission statement. They have had no guarantees. They run a competitive market, and I must say I accept their word above the word of someone who is not involved in this business.
The Government of Canada approach goes beyond the realm of good intentions as far as Canadian content is concerned. It should be remembered that the Canada-U.S. agreement stipulated that each government endeavour to ensure that the supply of goods and services to the pipeline project would be on generally competitive terms. Mr. Speaker, I do not think anybody in this country would want a pipeline built on non-competitive terms.
In its report giving Foothills the green light last summer, the National Energy Board said the company should develop its purchasing program so as to ensure that Canadians have a fair

and competitive opportunity to participate in all facets of the project. I stress the word competitiveness because that is all that can be reasonably asked in any market, at any time, that competitiveness be involved. It is also stipulated that the level of Canadian content be optimized as far as is practicable, and that maximum advantage be taken of opportunities provided by the project to establish and expand supplier firms in Canada.
I realize other members wish to speak in this debate, Mr. Speaker. I wish to conclude in this manner that, if we are convinced that it is the private sector of our economy which will provide the jobs many Canadians want, then surely it should be the object of all members of this House, regardless of what side they sit on, to ensure a project of this magnitude goes forward and that the stimulus of $4 billion in 1976 terms does occur within our economy.
It is foolish to discuss whether the regulations should be issued now, later or in between. A report should be made to this House through a committee every quarter. I would like this matter to go to committee and I would like to see this bill passed in order that those people involved in the construction of this project have the lead-in time required.
In Canada there are insufficient numbers of skilled workers should that pipeline construction commence tomorrow. Workers would have to be brought in. We need lead-in time to co-operate with the provinces to ensure that, if there is a shortage of skilled labour in this country, classes are set up immediately in schools so that when the pipeline project does proceed we will have the necessary people to provide that labour for those jobs. This will require the co-operation of the provinces and of the federal government.
Following the conclusion of the first ministers' conference last week I saw a ray of light across the country. Some of the opposition members have not learned what the premiers have learned, that it is more important at this time to get on with the job rather than bringing up straw issues because there may be an election this year or next year. The people of Canada do not want us to play politics with their futures. They want us to do what we were elected to do in the first place, which is to ensure that what is best for this country is carried out. The government has a monitoring position to ensure that it gives every assistance and encouragement to private industry.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to say something in this debate concerning the proposal of the Foothills Pipe Lines Company and its sponsors, Alberta Gas Trunk Line of Calgary and Westcoast Transmission Company of Vancouver. I would like to pay tribute first of all to these two sponsoring companies which are prepared to take on the largest single project ever proposed by private enterprise in Canada, in the United States, or indeed anywhere in the world. It takes a lot of personal and corporate courage, a lot of stamina and tenacity to do this, and particularly so in Canada today.
Round one of this contest ended last fall when the government made its decision in favour of the Foothills project to
February 21, 1978

build the line along the Alaska Highway instead of by way of the Mackenzie valley. I say to the House, Mr. Speaker, that the energies and efforts so far on the part of this group, Foothills and its sponsors, are likely to be minuscule in comparison to the tasks which now lie ahead.
One of the First and most important steps to be taken in our country is the passing of this legislation by parliament. Ministers of the government have been emphasizing the importance of quick passage of the bill which has been introduced. It is typical, however, of this government that an agreement signed by Mr. Schlesinger on September 24 and the required bill passed quickly through the United States Congress. It is now four and a half months later when it is before our parliament. The minister of energy and at times the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) have spoken in Canada about the urgency of energy matters but their actions have never supported their words. This has always been the case in every other matter relating to energy, whether it be northern regulations, agreements with the provinces, or taxation matters.
When I consider the project I have concern about government involvement, not the lack of it, but the over-abundance. This bill and other information available make it clear that Ottawa will be controlling every minute detail of the project. This has been demanded by the New Democratic Party too.
First of all the size of pipe was chosen by the National Energy Board, and thus the key technical specifications and ultimately the capacity of the line has been determined by the government. All of the rates and tariffs on the system and return on investment will be determined by the government. Property taxes on the line will be set by the government and it appears there will be a strong level of intervention over the control of purchasing policies of the company. The financing of the project and every detail of this important aspect will be controlled by the government. The government will be dictating labour policy, where the employees will be recruited from, how they will be qualified and, I presume, how much they will be paid. All of these things will be taken on by the government.
Who in the experience of Canada during the 1970's would have confidence in a government which is proven to be so inept, so slow to arrive at decisions, and so costly in their operations? Just the same, the route of the pipeline, and presumably every bend and twist, will be dictated by government. I applaud the Foothills Company and its sponsors for the willingness they have shown to accept this difficult and onerous demand upon them.
The thrust of the debate and the criticism of the project by the New Democratic Party have been almost solely concentrated on the question of more government control. In addition, this criticism has been demanding in absolute terms that every single man-hour, every pound of material or supplies, every valve, be spelled out precisely as to where it will come from, and at what cost.
Northern Pipeline
The party to my left has in fact taken a stand against the pipeline. This seems incredible in view of the position taken in the past week by Premier Blakeney of Saskatchewan, who is in favour of the project.
Last August all parties in this House supported in principle the proposal of Foothills to build this pipeline to deliver Alaska gas to the United States and perhaps to carry Canadian Arctic gas to markets by way of the Dempster route. The demands being made by the New Democratic Party are unreasonable and impractical. I say this as a businessman who has been involved from time to time in large projects, and I can tell you that it is never possible, especially when pioneering as is the case with Foothills, to be absolutely precise in every detail so far in advance.
The question really at this stage is whether there will be a pipeline or whether there will not be a pipeline. If the demands of the New Democratic Party were to be built into the legislation then it is my view that two problems would occur. The first one would be with the United States. I discussed this entire matter just last evening with a United States Senator. There are some misconceptions in the United States and Washington about this line. There is great concern about the undisclosed conditions imposed by the province of British Columbia.
The matter of gas pricing in the United States itself is perhaps the most important ingredient in enabling Alaska gas to move to the lower 48 states. Suffice it to say, while there was an agreement between Canada and the United States to build this line, we are by no means out of the woods, either in Canada or the United States.
The activities of most businessmen have one important ingredient, perhaps above all others, and in a $10 billion project the importance of bankers and financiers is more significant than in smaller undertakings. It is, however, important in any undertaking. I can say that all investors are fearful of investments which can be severely and adversely affected by bad government decisions, or in fact, no decisions, as well as by government regulation. One important policy which is needed in Canada, particularly as it relates to this project, must be predictable and certain rules where they must exist.
There is an opportunity to restore business and investor confidence, and respect in Canada and in the rest of the world for this Parliament. There is an opportunity to perform a meaningful part of the rescue necessary for Canada's economy. Let us face it, we require a boot strap operation.
This government, which had very little to say or propose at the first ministers' conference, did, however, highly tout energy projects for decades ahead. The problem is that long lead times of five, ten or 15 years are required to put major energy projects into operation. The result is that short term benefits, that is, during the 1970's, will not result from most of the plans that were outlined by the government.
There are one or two important exceptions, however, and at the top of the list is this proposal dealing with a natural gas pipeline from Alaska to the lower 48 states.

February 21, 1978
Northern Pipeline
If this project is to proceed without government backstopping, attractive and innovative proposals must be offered to investors. I believe that the greatest possible threat to the ultimate construction of the line is the difficulties that will no doubt be experienced when the details of financing are hammered out. This financing is by no means, in my view, a certainty, and thus, we in this parliament must, as far as reasonably possible, give to Foothills and its backers flexibility to work around the horrendous problems that lie ahead of them, not only in the banking but in the logistics, the negotiations with sellers of the gas, buyers of the gas, and with our own government agencies.
A great deal has been said about jobs; there are few in Canada, except perhaps this government, who would not say that this is a top priority. Members of this House, however, must recognize that if the choice is a pipeline or no pipeline, or
5,000	jobs rather than 6,000 jobs, or 90 per cent of the steel versus 100 per cent of the steel, then surely, there is no question that most of the pie for Canadians is better than none of the pie. To a large degree the question is the extent to which we Canadians and parliamentarians are prepared to place our confidence in the Foothills group of companies. If we are not prepared to do this, a decision in favour of those companies and their proposal should have been rejected out of hand last summer. I am a believer, however, that their track record and their stated intentions speak for themselves. It would be impossible to work out this project on the basis that every last detail be spelled out in advance. This is always desirable when relationships are developed between parties, even I suppose now-a-days by way of marriage contracts prior to committing to a spouse. I am convinced, however, that no amount of rules or regulations will be as important as the good will, the integrity, along with the willingness of the parties to co-operate and to compromise.I believe that the Foothills group in this regard has been outstanding. In fact I sometimes have concern that they have gone too far in accepting the demands of government.
On the matter of supply of materials by Canadians, I have some experience as one who has spent more than 25 years in an important segment of the oil and gas industry, not only in Canada but in the United States and in other countries. To begin with, a lot of the work that will be carried out on the pipeline will be carried out by the contractors who are the prime people in such an operation and, of course, many subcontractors.
I might tell the House a little about the pattern of American involvement in our Canadian oil and gas industry in the past. During the early part of the Canadian oil boom, from Leduc and in the years following, a large percentage of the drilling rigs in western Canada were owned by U.S. companies. The drilling superintendents and toolpushers on the rigs were in many cases American. There was a significant ingredient from Texas, California, and Louisiana. By the middle years of the 1950's, however, this changed, and this important part was probably 90 per cent Canadian owned before 1960.

What is perhaps even more important is that these same Canadian companies have carried their expertise as well as Canadian goods, technology, and experience to all corners of the world. A meaningful percentage of the wells drilled in Alaska has been drilled by Canadian companies based right in Calgary. The same is the case in California, Texas, Colorado, and the Rocky Mountain area of the United States. I say most emphatically that in this international industry, if Canadians take a parochial view, they could exclude themselves from a meaningful portion of international oil and gas activities.
When I look at the pipeline contracting group, those who have the expertise, I find names such as Majestic, Bannister, and Price, to name three. These companies have been established in Canada for a number of years and all of them employ Canadians virtually 100 per cent. They are ready, willing, and able to take on the task of laying this big-inch pipeline along the Alaska Highway.
Laying a 56-inch pipe is not going to be an easy task. There will be complications. It is a very large pipe and this size of pipe has never been laid before. It will require considerably larger ditches, different set-ups for welding, and there will be a good deal to be learned about bending and laying as well as new techniques which will have to be developed as we proceed. A supreme effort will be necessary if Canadian contractors are to train personnel. At the present time it is reasonable to predict there will be shortages of well-qualified people, particularly in areas of welding, fitting, and millwright work. Canadians must be trained and the companies should be prepared to fill every job with Canadians. There will, however, be a shortage of good people and an opportunity will thus be provided to every Canadian who really wants to work.
Any delay in the construction of this project would increase the probability of bunching the demands in the labour market. There are a lot of projects ahead and some of them have been mentioned in the past week or so, both by the first ministers and by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie). They include the construction of another Syncrude plant, a heavy oil plant in northwest Saskatchewan, and many other labour-intensive projects. Thus it is important that construction be kept on time and that no delays take place. Otherwise start-up problems will be plagued by labour shortages. Where possible every preference should be given to the employment of local personnel. I refer to the Yukon, British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan through which the pipeline is to run. I suggest that all those in Canada who want the opportunity to work will have the opportunity to do so.
We have heard a good deal about pipe and its supply for the pipeline. A considerable amount of know-how exists relating to pipeline and other oil-related projects, and it is likely that with appropriate lead-time and planning a significant amount of valves, fittings and all other requirements, particularly compressor station needs, can be supplied from Canadian fabricating plants. There is no doubt in my mind that the largest benefit will accrue to plants and manufacturers in central
February 21, 1978

Canada-Ontario and Quebec. But this project, because of its size, will have a tremendous impact, and a favourable one, on virtually every province in our country.
As we look at the projected activity, the central core it is certain will be Edmonton. Since the modern history of the west was written, Edmonton has been the embarkation point for northern Canada. The Alaska Highway was built during World War 11 and was staged from Edmonton. It was the base forearth-moving companies during early oil industry days when Swan Hills and Alaska Highway oil activities were under way. It has aviation companies, transportation companies and communication companies, as well as a large pool of trained personnel.
Alberta has built up a nucleus of pipeline and oil and gas engineers and technicians and welders since the first big-inch pipelines were laid in the early 1950's. A number of important Canadian pipeline companies were spawned as well during the 1950's; I think of such names as Westcoast Transmission, Interprovincial Pipe Line, TransCanada, the Alberta Gas Trunk Line, Trans Mountain and others. Their expertise and experience cannot be surpassed anywhere in the world. Most of the half dozen major pipeline contractors now based in Alberta have, over many years, qualified themselves as the best, most efficient, and economical builders anywhere in the world.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
In addition, through construction in northern Alberta, in British Columbia and in the Yukon these same companies have a wealth of knowledge about northern operating conditions. They are experienced in operating at extremely low temperatures, handling difficult logistics, and working with local labour in these areas, as well as touching at times permafrost construction conditions.
In Canada we have developed a number of vehicles specifically designed to serve the oil and gas industry. Some of these will be in heavy demand in the construction of the pipeline. I think of vehicles such as the Nodwell, the Skidoos, the snowmobiles coming from the province of Quebec, air-cushion vehicles and four-wheel drive vehicles especially equipped to deal with northern conditions, all of which will be required when the project goes ahead.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that Canada has not only the expertise to deal with this project. It has the experience, it has the companies, and it betters the qualifications possessed by other parts of the world including the United States. I therefore have no doubt that the Foothills group, which must seek competitive prices for its goods and services, will find substantial savings by dealing with Canadians virtually all the way. I do not, however, feel that any further demand should be placed upon the Foothills group to utilize any Canadian content greater than has already been spelled out by the government.
I listened carefully to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources yesterday when he spoke on the matter of Canadian energy supply. It now appears that the government has finally understood the problem. However, nothing it has done has indicated any capacity to deal with it. Obviously, all the
Northern Pipeline
potential energy projects which have been outlined are possible for the future. What is needed, however, is enabling legislation to make it possible for investors to proceed with the projects. Tax incentives with respect to tar sands projects, improved regulations affecting northern lands and so on, would provide the proper climate. All these things have been so slow in coming that our future energy supply has been prejudiced.
One of the facts of life, however, is that in the 1980's the price of crude oil will likely rise to $25 a barrel or more. At the same time the price of natural gas will track very closely. This will take place at a time when supplies of oil and gas from traditional OPEC sources will be tapering off, if they are available at all. The world today has become so dependent upon OPEC oil that massive power over the world economy has been transferred to those states. Canada and the United States, which today are the biggest energy per capita users on earth, sharing some 40 per cent of energy consumption, are in a very vulnerable position.
We in Canada are in precisely the same boat as the U.S. We are facing an increasing dependence in the decade ahead on imported energy from the OPEC countries. Alaska's Prudhoe Bay oil, which has been flowing for the last year, will relieve the problem to some degree. Alaska gas and gas from the Canadian Arctic will slow the trend toward increased dependence on imports. But even if rapid decisions are forthcoming with respect to transportation methods, financing and construction, supply of the resources involved is still many years down the road.
The fact is that by the mid-1980's Canada will be importing approximately half of its crude oil despite all the protestations by the government about energy self-reliance. The United States will be importing approximately half its oil, so our problems are almost identical. The development of the reserves in the Canadian Arctic and the considerable reserves in the North Sea will make an important contribution to the free world.
I point out, however, that if we are to have any leverage whatsoever with OPEC countries and with those who set the price, and if we want to be immune from world blackmail, it is absolutely vital that not only do we find reserves of oil and gas but also that we produce the transportation systems to bring them to market. Our frontier reserves are of absolutely no use to us whatsoever if they are locked under the permafrost and if no transportation system exists.
It has been stated many times before that Canada's present economic crisis, brought on by the Trudeau government opposite, might seem small in comparison if one adds the imports of perhaps 1.2 million barrels of crude oil a day in the 1980's at a price of close $25 a barrel. This would represent a further drain on our own foreign reserves in the order of $30 million per day or close to $10 billion a year.
Notwithstanding the animosity the government has shown to investors in recent years, surely there is a strong case to be made for increasing the return to Canadian or even American

February 21, 1978
Northern Pipeline
risk takers who are prepared to search for oil and gas reserves in our country, versus the alternative of paying exactly the same amounts to those in distant parts of the world where security of supply is so uncertain.
As I look at this proposed pipeline project I hope that in the years ahead we will see shares offered to Canadians. As we sat down with the financial experts who have been considering this it was explained that there is almost no equity market for shares in Canada at the present time, and the reasons are pretty obvious. Through tinkering as well as massive and destructive changes in our tax laws, the government has virtually driven Canadians from the ownership of their own country. There have been some improvements in recent years, but I say they have been far too little and far too late.
In the early 1960's in Australia there was a desire to have Australian participation in their own mining and oil and gas industries. That country made the purchase of shares in resource companies purchased from the treasuries of those companies fuly tax deductible. Literally tens of thousands of ordinary Australians had a stake, and in many cases a meaningful stake, in the resources of their own country. However, it takes bold and imaginative moves, not the picky little things our government comes out with every year or so and, as I say, far too little to get anything moving. It will take bold and courageous moves if problems regarding Canadian investment are to be solved.
On the question of security of supply, which I think is paramount to this whole matter, the Alaska Highway pipeline which will carry natural gas to American markets is almost as important to Canadians as it is to Americans. In the event of a national emergency or of a conventional war-and the Russians are building their conventional weapons at a rapid rate- there would undoubtedly be an urgent demand to devote all energy supplies to our mutual defence effort.
Due to Canada's complacent role in defence matters during the Trudeau years and because of the weapons capabilities of the United States we would have to turn to our neighbours to a large extent for our total defence and weapons needs. This means that we Canadians, in spite of our cold climate, would be faced with turning our thermostats down, perhaps to the freezing level, so that our protector, the United States, could undertake our mutual defence responsibilities. It is very much in our interests, therefore, that the United States properly manage its own energy policies. At times I have been concerned about whether the United States has done that or maximized its energy policies.
This Alaska energy artery is an important and vital contribution to the mutual defence needs of Canada and the United States. In addition, any alternative consideration, such as tankers to carry natural gas down the west coast, as is presently the case with Alaskan oil, in the event of war would be a disaster.
It must be remembered too that while 50 per cent of our oil needs during the 1980's will be met by imports from OPEC countries, this oil will be largely from Iran and the Middle East, thus traversing the sea lanes of southern Africa. This

security of supply is related to our ability to keep these routes open as much as it is to the willingness and ability of OPEC nations to continue supplying us with oil. The disastrous policies of the western and oil consuming nations, including Canada, relating to South Africa and Rhodesia add significantly to the uncertainties of our oil supply routes in the future.
As I look at the question of our relationship with the United States, I come back to 1941 when the Portland Pipeline was constructed from an American port to Canada as a war measure to supply Canada's Montreal refineries. This avoided difficulties as a result of the freeze-up of the St. Lawrence and the limited season, and it avoided a great many problems for Canada. This line, which travels about 160 miles through the United States, has carried, as recently as 1965, up to 550,000 barrels of oil a day, and it is presently putting through almost
400,000	barrels a day.
During the war when Canada was faced with oil supply problems the United States undertook to supply our domestic oil needs from its own short supply. There was one simple condition: that Canada ration on the same basis as the United States rationed its citizens.
At the present time a large portion of Canada's oil and gas from western Canada travels through the United States by way of the TransCanada Pipelines for gas and the Interprovincial Pipe Line for oil. There are further elaborate plans under way between our two governments to construct joint oil storage reservoirs on the east coast of Canada. The Alaska Highway pipeline project is just another element in this important master plan, but the point is that when the shoe was on the other foot and we were constructing pipelines to suit our needs and to preserve our security, the United States was there and co-operated willingly.
I would like to comment on the complex regulatory agency which the minister has proposed and he stated will be staffed by 200 people. It is interesting that this figure is precisely the figure given in this House by the then minister of finance at the time the Anti-Inflation Board was established. Within two years the staff of the AIB exceeded 900. The cost estimates of the AIB doubled in the first two years.
I think the government must place itself in the position of not asking what the Foothills group can do for it but what it can do for Foothills. If it does not, Foothills may fail. The pipeline may never be built. This massive and difficult undertaking will require a degree of industry and government cooperation never before seen in our country. In addition, the arranging of financing will be a massive undertaking. It will be difficult to accomplish, and some say even dicey in the outcome.
When I look at the bill before the House I believe that the greatest single potential obstacle to the project's going ahead may well be the unwillingness of bankers to produce a blank cheque to cover the costs of the northern pipeline agency. If the government's freewheeling spending patterns are any indication, this could be one of the largest, most uncertain and unfathomable costs in the total project.
February 21, 19 78

Hon. members and others must ask themselves if they would invest in or lend to a company which hands blank cheques over to this government. I will be proposing an amendment in the committee and a formula to limit the amount of cost which can be charged to Foothills for the activities of the regulatory agency.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, and the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) have made much of the Dempster connection. I say that there is an excellent chance that the Dempster lateral will never be built. I agree, however, that at the present time it is a good standby. It is perhaps the only standby alternative we have, but the Dome Petroleum Company, which has followed a courageous exploration course in the Beaufort Sea, appears now to have the reserves which could present a threshold level to construct what was originally proposed as the Mackenzie Valley pipeline. Notwithstanding this, however, it is also likely that early deliveries from this area will be by tankers, which require less than the threshold volumes required for a pipeline.
In conclusion, the proposal put forward by the Foothills company is simply for a transportation system. It is the transportation of energy in the form of natural gas, and the customer is the United States. This task is not dissimilar to the provision of transportation by other methods such as rail, ship, or air. In this case it is over a land bridge between states of the United States.
Transportation is big business in Canada, and so is the pipeline business. The latest years for which comparative data are available in this country indicate that pipeline transportation of oil and gas yielded revenues of $1.3 billion. This was 16 per cent of the combined revenue of the transportation of all goods by air, rail, ship and truck transport. Pipelines are nothing new in this country. In fact they have been around for more than 100 years. Today Canada has nearly 100,000 miles of pipeline, compared with some 60,000 miles of railroad track.
