The Interprovincial and TransCanada systems are respectively the world's longest oil and gas pipelines. These and other pipelines have provided Canadian engineers with tough challenges and the opportunity to pioneer technology. For instance, the Trans Mountain Pipe Line which carries oil from Edmonton to Vancouver, traversing both the Rocky Mountains and the coast mountain ranges, still today represents a remarkable engineering feat.
I believe that the contribution in dollars and cents to Foothills, a transportation company, for the task of transporting American gas is sizeable and impressive. Commencing with the first full year of the Foothills Alaska system, and excluding Dempster, it is projected that the company will realize a net profit of $170 million after tax. Total cash flow before tax and before depreciation will be in the order of $500 million per year. This is some 10 per cent of our present balance of payments deficit. The Government of Canada will collect in the order of $ 150 million per year in federal income
Northern Pipeline
taxes from the Foothills Company. Thus, over a period of ten years the income collected by the government will approach $2 billion from the company, and the contribution to Canada's balance of payments will be in the order of $50 billion.
When we have an opportunity to pass a bill in parliament to assist an enterprise of such tremendous importance to Canada as this, we had better not pick and debate matters which are insignificant in the total and may well contribute or result in the downfall of the entire project. We have an opportunity to demonstrate to the world that Canada is capable of undertaking the largest pipeline ever undertaken and completed in the world, in terms of dimension as well as total dollars. A positive and helpful approach is required on the part of parliamentarians and the government. A vital step is required by the Trudeau government to indicate to the investment community world-wide that the follies of this government are a thing of the past.
We have the opportunity to establish Canada's credibility as a country in which to invest. We have an opportunity to assist our neighbour and protector, the United States of America. That country is our largest trading partner. We can contribute significantly to our mutual energy and defence security.
Therefore let us move forward and not bicker over the division of the pie as to who receives 5 per cent or even 10 per cent more, one way or the other. Let us ensure that the pie is baked and the project goes ahead.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enter into this debate for a number of reasons. Before getting into the context of my address, however, I should like to make a few corrections to some of the comments made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson) earlier this afternoon. In fact he rather flattered me and the New Democratic Party, as he devoted almost his entire speech to criticizing what some of our members have said. When that happens on the government side of the House, then I know a lot of what has been said by members of the New Democratic Party must be correct, and government members must be somewhat worried.
He mentioned the problem of guarantees, which has arisen in a number of debates. Yesterday the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Young) indicated that we cannot have built-in guarantees that all material and manpower will be Canadian. My party is not demanding a guarantee that every person working on the job and every piece of material which goes into the project be Canadian. If one looks at the current world situation, it is patently obvious what we are concerned about. Of course one area is jobs. Top priority for jobs has to come from Canada. There must be Canadians working on that pipeline. That is paramount.
The other area is: when we are talking about guarantees we are not talking about unfair competition. We are not saying that Canadian corporations, whether it is Stelco, Ipsco or some other small producer, should be given a carte blanche opportunity to fleece the Canadian government, Foothills, or any other

February 21, 1978
Northern Pipeline
manufacturer or contractor involved in this project. We want to caution Canadians. Other countries such as Japan, Italy and Germany produce steel. In those countries steel corporations are heavily subsidized by their governments. Therefore we may end up in a situation where there is unfair competition and very unfair bidding when it comes to the pipeline and the various material components which go into it. This is what we are concerned about.
We are not asking for a special status for Canadian corporations in order for the price to be bid up in their contracts. We are not asking Canadian workers to demand exorbitant labour wage rates. We are asking for fairness and a close look at how corporations in other countries bid. That is our basic concern. I attempted to make that clear yesterday when I asked the hon. member for Niagara Falls a question at the termination of his speech.
Also we are very concerned about the environmental impact. I will have a great deal to say about that later on. As well we are concerned that some hon. members in both the Conservative and Liberal parties are criticizing and condemning the New Democratic Party for being opposed to the pipeline and, for some reason or other, being anti-American. Both of those criticisms are absolutely wrong. Members of the New Democratic Party are not anti-American. But when Canada enters into a deal with the wealthiest nation in the world, which saves that nation $6 billion, because it is not necessary to liquify gas and take it down the container route to the American west coast, and when it is indicated that the best deal possible has been negotiated, there is a question in my mind as to whether that is so.
After negotiations on September 23, 1977, Mr. Schlesinger, who is in charge of United States energy, indicated that the agreement is particularly advantageous to the United States by providing a ceiling on every aspect of potential United States liability, while creating new incentives for efficient construction on a portion of the project which would normally be subject to exclusive Canadian jurisdiction. That type of statement makes me somewhat suspicious that perhaps we did not get the right deal. Be that as it may, we are not opposed to the co-operation the government has entered into with the United States. We are concerned about the nuts and bolts, literally and figuratively speaking, of the entire operation. After all, this is the greatest financial undertaking of a project in the history of our country.
Whether or not the Liberals or the Conservatives have read their history, we know what happened when the other great project was being undertaken in this country back in the latter part of the nineteenth century, and what a hosing the Canadian public took at the hands of the CPR. What we are saying today is that we do not want the next generation or the generation after that to look back and say, "The men and women sitting in the House of Commons in the year 1978 sold us down the river". We want to prevent that kind of thing from happening. We want a fair and equitable deal with

Foothills and with the investors, and we want fair and equitable wages to be paid. We want the pipeline to be built, but we want to make sure that at least that portion that runs through Canada has top Canadian content and will benefit Canadians.
There is one thing we must keep in mind. I think many Canadians at present are under the illusion that this is a totally Canadian operation, that we will bring Canadian gas from the northwest to Canadian consumers. I am amazed at some of the phone calls I receive. Let us put it on the record that, initially and perhaps for the next 20 years, this project will be basically an American project, not Canadian. The project is to bring American natural gas through part of Canada to the United States. We are providing a service. We should have bargained in a much harder way with Mr. Schlesinger and with the U.S. government.
It is interesting to note that in the past three or four years the cost of natural gas to the consumer, to the home owner, and to the person who rents an apartment, has skyrocketed, and yet we have an over supply of natural gas in this country. The most reliable estimates say that we have enough natural gas to last us into the 1990's. What we are doing right now is providing a land corridor for U.S. natural gas to come through Canada to the U.S. I want to make that point very clear. If and when we need Canadian gas we will have to look again at the Dempster spur to find out whether or not we will build a pipeline at that time and to make sure that we can supply our own consumers with our own gas.
A few moments ago I mentioned the environmental aspects of the operation, of this giant project. Environment means two things: it means the physical or natural environment, and it also means the human environment.
I can recall growing up in northern Ontario. We lived in Sault Ste. Marie at the time of the great uranium boom at Blind River and Elliot Lake, Lake Lauzon, in that area, and I can recall the terrible social and economic upheaval at the time of the boom when hustlers and hucksters operated and the cost of a hot-dog shot up from 10 cents to 25 cents. Prostitutes walked the streets, taxi drivers doubled their fares, and houses of ill repute popped up all over the place at Blind River and Elliot Lake. The crime rate soared and the murder rate soared. The police force consisted of only two policemen in those days.
I remember my father talking to the chief of police who said he was literally afraid to go out in his patrol car on a Friday or Saturday night. At that time the cost of food and rents soared. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) will remember that when the pipeline was built in Alaska, the net or real income of people who lived in that corridor dropped because prices became inflated as a result of unscrupulous individuals who moved into the area to exploit the people who lived there.
The other aspect which is very important is native land claims. This is a very important subject which has been postponed for so long that it has almost become part of our history, and a very tragic part at that. I suggest to the minister that we should not proceed with the pipeline until we get at
February 21, 1978

least a memorandum of understanding from the native community. I am not suggesting that within the next few months we can settle all the land claims, but I think that there should be some agreement made before the first bulldozer goes in, although I understand that many of them have already gone into the area. I believe that native land claims are paramount at this time.
We all know what our forefathers did to the natives in that part of Canada. They stole their land, they squatted on it, they assumed title to it, and before they knew it it was theirs. This is why the native people of the Northwest Territories today will not tolerate that kind of intrusion and will not tolerate the shacktowns that develop during the building of a pipeline so that in 10 or 15 years' time they will end up with virtually no land at all. We have to keep that in mind.
Another thing we must ensure is a strong local labour content in the building of this pipeline. I am not suggesting for a moment that it is possible to supply all the experts from the Yukon or from the Northwest Territories, from northern British Columbia or indeed northern Alberta. What I am suggesting is that on-the-job training programs should be started, not six months from now or a year from now but right now. Those should be on-the-job training programs both in theory and in practice so that the native people there will have a fair chance in competing for the jobs that will be available in the construction of this tremendous project. Unless we do that we will create the same bitterness, the same hatred, and the same misunderstanding that were created in the process of many other projects in the history of our country, such as the CPR, the Elliot Lake development, and so on.
May I call it five o'clock, Mr. Speaker? I will continue after the supper adjournment.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ABATEMENT OF NOISE IN HUMP YARDS
speechtext:
that Bill C-224, to amend the Railway Act (noise abatement), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I should like to raise an acute environmental problem this afternoon, and that is noise occurring in rather special locations, certain large railway yards concentrated in eight metropolitan centres in Canada. These are known as hump yards. There is one in Edmonton, two in Toronto, and others throughout the country.
The problem is causing polarization in a number of communities, including my constituency of Scarborough East, between the community and the railways. Only in Edmonton are efforts being made to correct it. The CPR in Toronto is doing nothing. The alderman in my constituency receives complaints continuously from residents with respect to the noise. It is a problem that has to be addressed by the federal government since under our constitution railways are a federal responsibility.
Some people may wonder why I raise the question in the form of proposed legislation and not through some attempt at co-operative action. The reason is that there is no federal jurisdiction available over noise. The jurisdiction lies with the province. If the province wishes to do something about noise in the hump yards it is inhibited by the fact that it is the federal government's responsibility, and if the federal government wishes to do something about noise it is stalemated because it has no legal authority.
In face of the failure of the railways to make any attempt to tackle this noise problem I have turned to the only course left, a private member's bill. I hope hon. members will listen to my reasoning and send this bill to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.

We should get it clear in our minds what a hump yard is and what the particular noise problem is. A hump yard is a major classification yard where new trains are made up. Existing trains are broken apart and cars are put together in a new fashion.
The particular characteristic of a hump yard is that a man-made hill is built in these yards, perhaps the height of a three-storey building. Two locomotives push cars up this hill two or three at a time. There is a certain noise involved with the whining of the locomotives but that is not the real problem. Those cars roll down the other side of the hill by gravity at quite some speed on their way to any one of literally dozens of tracks where they bump into trains being made up, at speeds up to four miles an hour, forming new trains.
As the cars roll down the hill by gravity, large steels beams about the length of this chamber-in the Scarborough yards they measure 106 feet-rise up on both sides of the tracks and, operated by computer, squeeze in and out against the wheels as they run down the hill. They grip the wheels tightly but the wheels keep turning. They grip, release, grip, release, while the computer retards the speed so that the car will go to the end of the track to its final destination and bump into the train being made up, at exactly the right speed.
It is not difficult to imagine the noise called "wheel screech" as these steel beams rise up and grip the steel wheels of the cars. It is steel on steel. There is a vibration sound, a high pitched screech, which reaches the threshold of pain in terms of decibels. Fortunately, it diminishes over a distance.
There are practical means of reducing this wheel screech. My point is that the CPR in Scarborough does not use the available practical technologies for reducing the noise. It is true that scientists have not yet told us exactly what produces the noise. We do not know if it is the retarder, if it is in the wheels, or if it is the vibration between the two. For our purposes it is not necessary to have the practical explanation of the noise. It is sufficient for our purposes to know that the noise level is intolerable and that it can be reduced by available technology which is not being used.
If the railways, which have the primary responsibility, do not undertake to utilize the available technology on the grounds that they were there First and the homes have been built since, or on the grounds that their major responsibility under the Railway Act is to provide transportation, or that reduction of noise does not eliminate it, then they are not co-operating.
The practice followed by our own federal Ministry of Transport of seeking a co-operative approach between the municipalities, the railways and the departments of environment in the provinces, will not work. It will not have credibility unless there are legal sanctions which can be used.
My bill is a practical means of giving legal power to the Canadian transportation commission-the regulatory agency-to back up the federal government which has no authority over noise at the present time. That is the purpose of the bill.
February 21, 1978

Let me explain the major provisions of this bill. They are not very difficult. This bill would be an amendment to Section 215 of the Railway Act. It would be known as "Abatement of noise in hump yards". It is focused, not on railway noise in general, but on those eight hump yards in Canada. It would give the Canadian Transport Commission the power, after looking at each situation, to direct the railway company to construct and maintain works for the abatement of noise emanating from hump yard operations which, in the opinion of the commission, caused a severe noise problem adversely affecting the community.
Secondly, the noise must be capable of significant reduction by the use of available technology. Measurements are not mentioned. It says, "Is there a noise problem?" If there is a problem, is available technology not being used? And if there is, the commission could order it to be installed. The bill would provide in the language that is appropriate to a private member's bill since we cannot call for expenditures of funds, that the transportation commission could, if it felt advisable, request the Ministry of Transport to contribute up to 30 per cent of the cost of the noise abatement works in the hump yard.
It also provides that if a municipality is an applicant for noise abatement, before proceeding the municipality would be required to agree that it would participate up to a maximum of 10 per cent of the cost of noise control. There is no authority for the federal agency to direct a municipality to spend money. All it says is if a municipality requests noise abatement works it ought to be prepared to participate in a small way because it controls the zoning which brings residences into the area.
Finally, the bill will provide that research into acoustic problems could be ordered with the federal government sharing, upon the request of the CTC, up to 50 per cent of the cost of new research into noise abatement. That is what it says. It is authority to the regulatory agency which at present has no authority over noise. We know for example that the regulatory agency can order the railways to spray weeds on the railway tracks and to remove weeds, to build fences and other things. It cannot say anything about noise. We are left helpless by the negative attitude shown on the part of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The Canadian National Railways has co-operated.
What technologies are available? For example, sound baffles could be built along the length, 100 or so feet, of the steel beams that rise up on both sides of the tracks, to soften the noise. Tests prove these baffles will reduce the noise by some 25 decibels, which is around 40 per cent of the total noise at the point of the noise emission. That is a significant reduction. Should the railway employ that technology if the community is affected adversely? I think it should. If it does not and we say "Let's co-operate" and it fails to co-operate, where is the lever? We do not have one. My bill simply says put in a lever which will give credibility to our responsibility in railway functions to handle this question.
There are other technologies available, some of them good and some of them not so good. For example, an oil and water emulsion has been sprayed on the wheels to help deaden the
Noise Abatement
noise, which has had some effect. There are other methods described in technical bulletins which are now available. The Burlington Northern Railway and the Westinghouse Brake Shoe company have done significant research in noise reduction in these special circumstances.
We know that railway classification yards, even though they have moved outside of the major urban centres, are now inside as urban growth takes place. Fifteen years ago in my constituency when zoning made possible this railway hump yard, noise was not the serious community concern that it is today. We must face it in today's terms. When zoning was put in for the railway hump yards there was also zoning for residential uses, homes that were not yet built. Houses are now there and the noise problem is with us. I am seeking a way of coping with it. Is the province doing anything about it?
The Ontario provincial ministry of transport and the CPR convened a seminar one year ago on the subject of railway noise. They concluded that it was a matter for a federal authority. We have no authority because of the gap in our legal capacity.
The province of Ontario is currently issuing new regulations covering new homes in the Malvern area and around the hump yard in Scarborough East. These new regulations deal with sound baffles in new communities, in the siting of homes, in earth berms to break the noise and in heavier insulation in the homes. It has been estimated by some that the cost to homeowners and developers will be between $2,000 to $3,000 per home to meet the noise problems of highways and railway yards.
Can we leave the railways without responsibility to act when the province is acting, when the municipality has zoned the area residential at the same time that it is zoned industrial for the yards, and when this new problem of noise emerged?
In conclusion, this bill is an effort to provide the federal authority through its regulatory agency with the legal power to research a noise situation only in the hump yards. I am not taking a broad approach. It may then order remedial works to reduce noise if there is technology available and it is not being used. It may request the government to share in the cost and it may, if a municipality has applied, ask that municipality to share in the cost in a minor way. It may sponsor and pay some costs of research into noise reduction. I hope it will commend itself to my colleagues in the House and that they will agree to send it to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications where the federal Departments of Transport, Northern Affairs, Environment, the provincial departments and railways can be called to explain their role in the present situation.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ABATEMENT OF NOISE IN HUMP YARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity to thank the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell) for bringing forth Bill C-224. We have had the same problem in the Edmonton-Calder area for many years. In 1969 and 1970 the same issue came up in the Edmonton-Calder area. There was the squealing of steel on
80031-S3'/2

February 21, 1978
Noise Abatement
steel in the hump yard which could be heard within a radius of approximately 30 miles. The unfortunate part of the problem was that most of the boxcars came in at one, two and three o'clock in the morning when people were sleeping. It was difficult to get the culprit, CNR, to do something about it. We did manage to get them to build barriers around the trackage for something in the neighbourhood of three miles. This is the buffer for the area.
Every two or three years, I receive letters from my constituents telling me it is time I started getting after the CNR again because they are not doing their job properly. There is a continuous program of the CNR together with the Department of the Environment, both in the federal and provincial field, which checks the decibel rate as far as this particular hump yard is concerned. I think the only solution is the one the hon. member mentioned. I will not go into it because he has described the whole process.
At one time this was on the outskirts of the city. It is now in the middle of an urban area. This is as a result of urban sprawl. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the question can be put one minute before six o'clock, there is a good chance this bill can be passed.
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for allowing me to speak and I am pleased to take this opportunity to make a few comments on second reading of Bill C-224, which contains amendments to the Railway Act and aims at reducing noise. I am happy to support the bill and I would like to offer my sincere congratulations to its author, the distinguished hon. member for Scarborough East.
I am well aware of the reasons which brought the hon. member to move this bill. I must admit frankly in the House that 1 have not discussed this bill with the hon. member for Scarborough East, but I will show in my comments that we are of the same mind and that the hon. member was motivated basically by the same reasons that would have moved me to introduce a bill somewhat similar to this one. When you have grown up near a railway, when your father was a railroad worker and when you yourself have worked for a railway during your summer vacation, it is easy to understand the importance and the complexity of the problem that the hon. member for Scarborough East would like to rectify today.
Of course, we could talk for several weeks about noise in general and for several days about noise caused by various railway activities. If we talk too long about this and do not choose to act as soon as possible and do what is required to correct the various sources of noise pollution, we would greatly compromise our credibility as parliamentarians. Some jokers would even accuse us of adding to noise pollution.
I understand very well that the hon. member for Scarborough East wished to concentrate his efforts on only one aspects of this source of pollution even though he could have mentioned many others.
This immediately brings to mind the CPR's engine whistles and the CNR's locomotives. In my home town, Grand Falls in New Brunswick, they wake up the people twice a night between twelve and 6 a.m., practically seven days a week. There are three level crossings in less than a mile, so we may easily understand the anger of citizens waking out of peaceful sleep, babies crying, children in tears in this small town with a
6,000	population.
Mr. Speaker, in this day and age I understand the concern of the bill's sponsor for public protection against the noise from railway hump yards or the unending movement of cars going through automatic retarders. The hon. member brought this particular problem to our attention because he figured this problem could be solved more easily through a bill. He explained a moment ago why we should amend the Railway
February 21, 1978

Act. As many other hon. members, he has gone through the frustrating experience of trying to put the problem before MOT officials, railway companies and the CTC. He has been confronted with repeated refusals from all quarters, because nobody wanted to take final responsibility for instituting remedies or taking the decision of solving the problem once and for all, and as fast as possible. This is why he had to put this legislation before Parliament. This is why I am in full sympathy with him.
I went through that kind of frustration, Mr. Speaker, when 1 endeavoured unsuccessfully to put an end to the nightmare of night-time engine whistles in Grand Falls. I could refer to countless letters showing that the legions of Julius Caesar would be needed to overcome the barrage and often fictitious impediments put up by the federal bureaucracy. I understand the hon. member for Scarborough East, after being confronted with that kind of refusals, having used all possible approaches, had to prepare this legislation as a last resort to solve the problem and that of the constituents he is so aptly representing here.
I wonder however if the hon. member would widen the scope of his bill to include all sources of noise pollution from railway operations, which are a real nuisance to the public and this is putting it reasonably.
And to think that the locomotive was invented in 1803, that the noise has not really diminished since then, and that we have not found a way to lessen the noise created by automatic retarders, or to silence those blasted night train whistles, taking into account for security reasons at level crossings: one cannot talk obviously of astounding technological advances, and that is certainly not to the honour of our railway companies or the Canadian Transport Commission which completely wash their hands of this situation.
The hon. member for Scarborough East and myself should perhaps invite the members of the Canadian Transport Commission and the boards of the railway companies to sleep every night for a week near either hump yards or in my native town of Grand Falls which is crossed by two railroads. Perhaps that would shake them out of their bureaucratic lethargy, and prompt them to set up a task force which would examine seriously these and other sources of noise caused by the railways and which, one must emphasize, considerably lower the quality of life of many Canadians, and many Canadian communities. I know of some commissioners who would simply say: But you don't have to live near a railroad, ladies and gentlemen. They are probably the ones who live comfortably in the high-class sections of Ottawa West, Alta Vista or Rockliffe.
The time has come to have the Canadian Transport Commission and railway companies carry out fully their duties and obligations toward the Canadian community.
For too long members of this House had to be satisfied with answers like: It is a known fact that the use of locomotive whistles in certain areas like Grand Falls poses a few problems for the people in the area. This is the kind of dumb answer we get from the Canadian Transport Commission. So there is a
Noise Abatement
whole lot of small but very annoying problems to be solved and it is time that someone dealt with them seriously. The Canadian Transport Commission must stop shunning its responsibilities and stop using arguments like: We are not empowered to change the requirements. Any amendment to those requirements must be made through an act of Parliament.
Is the commission really responsible for those many problems and complaints it receives regularly relating to noise pollution, did it point those problems out to the government, did it discuss them with the Minister of the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang)? Not that I know. If it did, how is it that in 1978, 171 years after the locomotive was invented, we have to put up with the noise made by whistles or automatic retarders in railway hump yards, in the middle of the night to bother everybody? Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to take a minute or two to deal with sub-clause (2) of clause 215.1 of the bill introduced by the hon. member for Scarborough East on municipal financial commitments as contributions to the solution of problems relating to the noise generated by railways.
A large and wealthy area like Toronto or Scarborough can afford to pay for part, even a very tiny part, of the cost but several small municipalities across Canada which are too poor and without good taxation resources do not have the budgets to pay for any part of the cost of installation of such equipment, no matter how small it is. Yet the formula presently contained in the Railway Act is applied evenly all across Canada, irrespective of the capacity of the municipalities to pay. Poor municipalities, we are sorry to say, are still going to have to put up with the noise of screechy locomotives for many years to come.
Even if this bill is not referred to a committee of the House for further consideration this afternoon-and I sincerely hope it will be-I think we will have accomplished something useful: we will have identified a serious problem and asked the federal government, its departments, its agencies, its commissions, provincial authorities and municipal governments to use the enormous research resources we have in this country for the solution of the problems we raised this afternoon.

I am familiar, in some measure, with the problem which confronts him. I recall the situation which arose in connection with my own private bill last session; the hon. member is attacking a different aspect of the same class of problem. The dilemma is this: The use of railway facilities in increasing and

February 21, 1978
Noise Abatement
at the same time communities across the country are continuing to grow. The two trends are not being co-ordinated. In my own case, in Scarborough West, the railway was planning to expand its marshalling yards, a process bound to result in increased noise, greater danger to traffic, higher pollution levels and so on. Yet no notice of this intention was given to the area in advance, just as I am sure no warning was given to people in the neighbourhood of hump yards that construction was due to take place. speakeroldname: Mr. Charles Lapointe (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ABATEMENT OF NOISE IN HUMP YARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the unfortunate duty of now speaking until the end of the period. In ordinary language, the tactic of speaking to a private bill until six o'clock is known as killing the bill. The expression is not very pleasant, but I think that for reasons I shall have the opportunity of mentioning later on in my speech, because of the difficulties the application of such a bill would entail, unfortunately I feel that it would not be easy to implement the bill proposed here by the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell). However I do think that this debate on the important matter of noise pollution in marshalling yards is very important, and that it should be held because, as the hon. member pointed out, some big companies at times turn a deaf ear to the problems of the citizens in a given area, and in this case, the citizens who live close by the shunting yards of railway companies.
The problem resulting from the noise caused by the various means of transport in residential areas is inevitably worsening with the simultaneous growth of transport and urban areas, two phenomena whose coexistence is marked by numerous problems. The considerable efforts made to reduce the noise of airplanes certainly do not have their counterpart in the field of railways, and as the hon. member for Scarborough East pointed out technology is not quite as advanced in that field as it is in that of aeronautics.
However this problem is serious, particularly in some areas like Edmonton as the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski) said, or in any other area where you have those hump yards. And the circumstances justify a debate on this matter today, Mr. Speaker, so that those corporations become more responsible and ready to co-operate more than they do now.
As the hon. member said in his remarks, there have been some initiatives or technical adjustments on the part of the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific to reduce noise in co-operation with the Ontario Department of Environment which has sponsored a conference to study the best means to reduce noise in hump yards but there is no satisfactory solution yet.
However, the seminar held last year has been the occasion of a positive exchange of views that has helped clarify the issue. Mr. Speaker, I think that this seminar is a good example of co-operation between railway company representatives and provincial, municipal and regional officials who met to find a practical answer to a mostly technical problem.
I am also pleased to mention that the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell) has taken himself a very active part in this research. The hon. member also had many discussions with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) on that important issue and through such forum and dialogues between all interested parties and at every level we should find technical solutions to deal with that problem in spite of its complexity. However, we cannot find a remedy without a better understanding of those real and increasing problems. First we should establish their origin and who is responsible for them, whether the railways, urban centres or urban planning. And I think that by continuing our research in that direction we will eventually end up by finding out the best means to solve these problems. These difficulties arise, Mr. Speaker, in the shunting yards, particularly those related to the industrial use of lands and residential areas when shunting yards and residential areas grow simultaneously and close to one another.
Such situations can happen because urban planning is the prime responsibility of the provinces and the municipalities while railway companies fall under the jurisdiction of the federal government and are not therefore subject to provincial laws. So sometimes-and unfortunately all too often-we witness a lack of coordination when it comes to getting an integrated urban planning system. Consequently, as the hon. member pointed out, conflicts may arise and actually do. Given the fact that planning affecting land is primarily the responsibility of the provinces, they should be in a position to see to it that no parallel development of land takes place when they are incompatible. However, as I mentioned previously, the two national railway companies are not subject to provincial laws. The federal government is then indirectly involved in issues relating to the use of urban land, if we may say so. This is why when he studies a request by Canadian National to obtain permission to build new facilities the Minister of Transport requires that the company back its request by letters from the municipality or municipalities involved as well as letters of authorization from Environment Canada before moving any further toward granting the request. Because of the nature of

February 21, 1978

their services, railway companies would rather build their shunting yards in industrial areas which are closer to the users of the means of transportation.
However this is not always possible, even in the case of shunting yards which originally were not located in residential areas. Problems have sprung up with the extension of the residential zones as well as with the extension or changes that railway activities have themselves undergone, beyond all expectation. In the present circumstances, we can classify the noise problems deriving from shunting operations into two groups: those that already exist and those that can be avoided if necessary action is taken.
Mr. Speaker, the legislation which is submitted today to the House suggests a legislative solution to the existing problems. The hon. member moved to amend the Railway Act in a way which would give the Canadian Transport Commission authority to direct the railway companies to take measures for noise abatement. The bill also provides for a cost sharing agreement among railway companies, the federal government and the municipalities but there is no mention of provincial financing.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier such federal legislative action would give rise to some difficulties. First, although several groups have suggested various steps to reduce noise in shunting yards and even if there was a symposium on the problem, as mentioned a while ago, current technology is not sufficiently advanced to warrant compulsory enforcement. It would be difficult to compel railway companies to apply those procedures without the necessary technology to do so effectively. If we compel railway companies to use the most recent technical methods, however inadequate they may be, nobody will be satisfied because the problem will not be entirely solved in spite of huge expenses. In short, Mr. Speaker, I think our intervention would be premature and would not allow us to achieve the objective we have set for ourselves.
The responsibility for the real origin of the problem and consequently the measures to be taken to correct it are controversial or at least very complex issues. Railroad companies are the source of the noise but they are not solely responsible for the various decisions which have been made and have led to conflicts between them and municipalities with regard to that ecological factor. So it seems to me that those companies should not be forced to defray the noise abatement costs. Municipalities or provinces, or both, should also accept responsibility for the problems stemming from the coexistence of marshalling yards and residential areas since they allowed that promiscuity. Although this matter does not really fall within its jurisdiction, the federal government should become involved in it to the extent that it encourages the railway companies to discuss their plans with municipalities.
This incentive has now become an obligation through a legislation introduced by our colleague from Scarborough East. From now on railway companies must advise the public of the proposed extension or changes to their facilities. People who live near these facilities now have the opportunity to express their views on these projects. Therefore the noise problem of hump yards in residential areas will be reduced
Noise Abatement
because the railway companies will have to discuss their projects as well as their possible effects with municipal authorities.
CP Rail went deliberately further in the pursuit of this spirit of co-operation by sponsoring the conference which was held in May 1977 and by spending, without being forced to do so by any legislation, $1 million to replace the equipment of Agin-court hump yard in order to reduce the noise caused by wheels. Mr. Speaker, I think we should express the hope that the spirit of co-operation which was shown at Agincourt by CP Rail will be pursued and accelerated, as requested by the hon. member. Railway companies have often shown their willingness to take appropriate steps to reduce the noise nuisance from which the people who live along the facilities suffer, provided municipal authorities are prepared to co-operate, to share the cost and to admit that the noise problems are not always due to railways.
Many factors are involved in the impact of a noise level on a community. The importance of each factor varies in each case and all the effects are not known yet. Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, unanimity has not been reached as to what noise levels are acceptable in one residential area or another. It is less than likely that a legislation or a standard might be equally applied in all cases. For example, it would be extremely difficult to draft a general list of standards which would apply in any situation. The other solution proposed would be to give wide ranging authority to some regulating body as the Canadian Transport Commission.
However, this body would not have the necessary authority to control all parties involved. For example, the commission could give orders only to federal bodies but not to the provinces or their bodies responsible for planning and problems related to land use. Considering these technical and jurisdictional uncertainties, it would be difficult to achieve this objective through legislation. The Canadian Transport Commission does not have the necessary authority to order provinces or municipalities to spend money, although, I believe, these are partly responsible in land use conflicts.
For the Canadian Transport Commission to consider the participation of a municipality, it would have to conclude beforehand an agreement with the railway company and the municipality concerning the cost sharing procedures. According to the bill, the commission can order a municipality to spend money only if it is one of the parties having filed a request. The other solution would be the establishment of a cost sharing fund similar to the fund for relocating railroad tracks or railway crossings; this solution is proposed in the bill.
This solution would entail the establishment of evaluation, budgeting and project control procedures and coordination with the provinces and other interested parties. But in the past the provinces have not approved cost sharing programs such as the fund for relocating railroad tracks and railroad crossings because it forces them to spend money in areas which are not in their priorities. Taking into account the dissatisfaction of the provinces towards the present sharing cost fund, it is not likely that such a procedure might be used. It seems, Mr. Speaker, that a federal legislation is not the ideal solution to

February 21, 1978
Noise Abatement
the problem raised by the hon. member today. We should rather endeavour to do research on the control and reduction of noise levels and to obtain better co-operation from the parties concerned. Of course, the federal government has a role to play in this area.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I was saying earlier in my address to the House this afternoon-and I want to re-emphasize this at this time-contrary to what some members on the government side may think, the NDP is not opposed to the pipeline. We are not opposed to most of the agreements that have been entered into. But we are deeply concerned about Canadian content, the not unreasonable guarantees that Canadian workers get the biggest share of the work market, and because it is a Canadian enterprise that Canadian corporations get a fair chance at bidding on contracts. As I said earlier, we do not want to see the Canadian taxpayers fleeced through some kind of phony guarantee situation whereby Canadian corporations, large or small, can inflate their prices and overbid on contracts.
Let me reiterate for a moment what I said before the supper break. We have a strong suspicion-in fact, it is more than a suspicion; we know-that steel corporations and other manufacturing firms related to this kind of huge project are heavily subsidized in countries such as Japan, West Germany and Italy. We want to make sure that our own companies and corporations, and flowing from them the workers of Canada, have an opportunity for fair bidding. There should be some kind of control mechanism built into this legislation to make very sure-I do not know exactly how this could be done internationally, but at least it is something for the government to consider-that we as a government know whether or not a corporation in Japan, Italy, West Germany, England or any other country, is giving us an honest bid; and by that I mean wage rates, interest rates and productivity rates that are relative to Canada. Unless our government knows exactly how the competitors have arrived at their figures, Canadian corporations and hence their employees will be in jeopardy.
February 21, 1978

There is one point I wanted to raise before the supper adjournment regarding a few comments that were made by some of my friends in the Conservative party about letting the free enterprise system operate in this project, letting the independent corporations compete and letting the chips fall where they will, in the hope that Canadian corporations will get a great deal of the work and the contracts. However, I did not hear any member of the Conservative party-I may be wrong-mention the fact that when Canadian corporations, great or small, find themselves in financial difficulties, it may not be their own fault. In fact, in many cases in the last two or three years it has been the fault of the government.
When they find themselves in financial difficulty, Mr. Speaker, where do they go? They may go to their bank or they may go to their shareholders and stockholders; but ultimately if they are in trouble they come to the government, whether it is the federal, provincial or municipal government. They come to the public purse and say: "Unless we can get some financial assistance from the various federal or provincial programs, we will go broke, we will go into receivership".
I am not personally opposed to this. If a company is potentially economically viable but is running into hard times within a few months or perhaps a year and a half, in such cases I think it is the duty of the country to assist that corporation. But what I dislike about what I have heard from some members of the House in both the Conservative and the Liberal parties is that one would think that the only people who come running to a government agency, whether it is for welfare, unemployment insurance or the Industrial Development Bank, are the down and outs, people who have been laid off or who are on welfare. I want to state now for the record that personally I am not opposed to government hand-outs to business which will assist the business to remain viable; but I am opposed to hearing only one side of the story, which is what happens very often in the House.
A few years ago this party coined the phrase "corporate welfare bum", and I know it hurt a lot of people. I do not want to refer to the corporate sector or to any individual as a corporate individual bum. I just want to point out that when corporations or individuals find themselves in trouble these days, they go to government. As members of parliament we know that, because they come to us for assistance.
Earlier this afternoon I spoke of the social problems that will affect people living in the Yukon. I do not profess to be a specialist in the social environment of the Yukon but I have read something about it and I have been there. When I was in my teens I saw what happened at Elliot Lake, Blind River, Spragge and Cutler and other places in northern Ontario during the uranium boom. I also saw what happened after the boom when the economy dropped to nothing. During the boom hucksters and hustlers came in, made a fast buck and the cost of living went up. That is one thing that I hope will not happen to native born Yukoners and people from southern Canada who have made their homes there.
Northern Pipeline
This bill should provide for some kind of agency not only to monitor the cost of the pipeline but to monitor the cost of living and social effects of the pipeline on the Yukon. I sincerely hope we will also go a lot further in settling land claims before the pipeline gets under way.
We have heard a great deal about the financing of the pipeline. Members on both sides of the House agree that this is an important matter and that we should get on with it. But I emphasize that we must be cautious. We must not march into what could be a huge, horrendous undertaking without certain guarantees for the Canadian people. I am not talking now in terms of narrow nationalism. I suppose the fashionable word today is nationhood, or love of nationhood, as propounded by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). Love of nationhood refers not only to Quebec but to Ontario, the maritimes and certainly the Yukon. We must make sure that the people of the Yukon understand they are an integral part of this country and that people from southern Canada are not going north to exploit them, to rip the shirts off their backs, whether they be native born Inuit or others living there.
We must make it plain that we are there for two reasons: first, to develop a gas pipeline to deliver United States gas to that country through Canada. The second reason is that eventually, perhaps 10 or 20 years hence, the pipeline might benefit Canada even though we have an abundance of natural gas at the present time. In my riding consumers complain that their natural gas costs have been mounting in the last two or three years. I do not think that even the economists can understand that unless it is because of the cost of delivery via the TransCanada pipeline.
When we talk of a pipeline, Mr. Speaker, we talk of development, development which will affect most Canadians. I hope it will provide needed jobs and an opportunity for investment in our country for those people who have the money. Unfortunately, the vast majority of Canadians do not have the money to invest. For that I blame this government which has been in power since 1963. That is the main reason that the majority of Canadians do not have money to invest. Members of the government can talk all they like about being proud of this country, investing in this country and all the rest, but people just do not have the money to invest in a pipeline.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) made an excellent speech in the House last evening. It was a business oriented speech. 1 stand to be corrected but, in effect, he said: "My speech is based on making money." He did not mean making money himself, of course. He went into all the arguments of how a pipeline could be financed. He spoke of the average Canadian taking pride in developing this great undertaking. If my memory serves me correctly, one thing he omitted to mention, however, was that probably 80 per cent or 90 per cent of Canadians will never have the opportunity to contribute financially to the pipeline and get a decent return on their investment. It will be left to a few people, groups of people, consortiums or organizations, to make money if there is money to be made. And I am quite

sure, Mr. Speaker, that there is money to be made eventually in this undertaking.
The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) says that the government is committed to maximizing the economic benefits of the pipeline to Canada. Mr. Speaker, if the government wants to do that why are there no provisions for Canadian content or Canadian jobs in the negotiated agreement with the United States or in this legislation? I know the word "guarantee" is a nasty one to free entreprisers and to entrepreneurs except when it comes to guaranteed loans from the government; then it is a different story.
I think this is endemic to this country. On the one hand we want to develop our great resources, but the financial imput comes from a very few people and the benefits go back to a very few people. The increase in the price of gas and oil today is an example. We are supposed to have an abundance of gas. However, we are told to be patriotic about it. The New Democratic party is criticized for being anti-American and against the pipeline. Mr. Speaker, we are not. This party is for the people of this country. We want a share in that as much as anybody else. We must address ourselves to that point and that point alone.
We are not intending for a moment to hold up this legislation. It is very interesting to note that we are being labelled in the press as the party which is filibustering; I am not pointing my finger at any specific colleague in this House. Granted there are only 16 NDP members in the House, but if you look at the list of speakers there are just as many Liberals and Conservatives speaking in this debate as there are New Democrats. So I hope the press will realize that it is not we who are filibustering this bill. We want to extend to this House constructive criticism. We do not want to stop construction of the pipeline; we want to make sure there are basic guarantees that will benefit Canada. What is wrong with being patriotic either at this time-or, for that matter, at any other time in the history of our country-when we are being torn asunder vis-a-vis Quebec and the rest of Canada?
What happens after the pipeline is built? It is not for me to delve into the financial details because I am not an expert in economics. There may be 2,000 to 2,500 people working on this pipeline, but what happens after it is finished? Is it going to be the same old story? Are we to have the same old shanty towns we had before in other parts of Canada? Are we going back to the days of Charlie Chaplin and the gold rush-the dog eat dog approach to the development of this country? It makes great poetry. Charlie Chaplin became a hero in the short time he lived in the Yukon. Surely today we can organize ourselves better as far as the social and personal implications are concerned.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that those who ultimately become powerful in regulating the development of this pipeline will make sure that the human aspect is taken into consideration, and I am quite sure the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) shares this point of view. I hope that by regulation, an

act of parliament or by changes or amendments to this bill, there will be guarantees not only of Canadian input but guarantees against human exploitation. To me this is just as important as manufacturing pipe and creating jobs.
When it is all over the people of the Yukon and the northern part of British Columbia will still be there. They will have to live with the remnants of a boom era. If that boom era is similar to what happened in other parts of Canada, such as Elliot Lake and Blind River, then the toll in human terms will be almost unbearable.
I spoke for approximately 15 or 20 minutes before the supper break and I will not take up too much more time. The New Democratic Party does not want to prolong this debate. We will have amendments to present in committee. This pipeline will be the greatest development this country has ever known, both in financial and human terms. I hope we do not end up with the same kind of package which our forefathers ended up with respecting the CPR-a sellout to the pioneers of this country. I am referring to the western pioneers, of course. I hope the day will not come when the people of the Yukon and northern parts of Canada will say: "You sold us down the river", or in this case "down the tube". I hope we will use this development as a unifying force in the country, not as a divisive force.
I hope we will also be able to benefit Canadians. Let there be no mistake, Mr. Speaker, we have nothing to fear from the United States. They are close friends. Geographically they are along our border. Seventy-five per cent of all Canadians live within 100 miles of the United States. Americans are tough bargainers. American businessmen respect toughness in negotiations and bargaining. I believe we have not been tough enough in negotiating this agreement with the United States. Mr. Schlesinger and other members of Mr. Carter's cabinet believe they got a better deal than we did. You cannot have respect for somebody who caves in. You cannot have respect for a relative or a neighbour who says: "Fine, go ahead, we will take this, you take that", and so on. I am not trying to be a prophet but I predict that in the long run Canadians will realize in seven or 10 years that this was not the best of deals, although I am not saying that their comment will be that it was the worst of deals. If we are not tough with our friends to the south, then as the Toronto Star said in its major editorial with respect to foreign ownership, I believe in yesterday's edition-this does not relate to this bill but I think it is cogent-"We can do better on our own".
This comment means we must make it abundantly clear to our friends to the south that we are second class North American citizens. We have resources. We have oil, natural gas, water, timber and all kinds of base metals. We have to bargain on an equal basis. Just because Americans outnumber Canadians 10 to one in population, and because their economy is bouncing back because of government intervention, something the Canadian government has been extremely reluctant to do, we should not take second place. We should bargain as North Americans sharing a continent, and making sure we get

That is democracy. We are members of parliament as well as those on the other side.
Northern Pipeline
The hon. member for Brant indicated he has some reservation with regard to the benefits of this pipeline to Canadians. I will touch on that later. I would also like to deal with the speech of the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Bawden) whose remarks I was privileged to hear earlier. I was encouraged by the positive approach that he took with regard to this major project which will have such an important impact on the Canadian economy in the years ahead. The way his party is now supporting this project is indeed an interesting turnaround.
When this session resumed after the new year, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) indicated that in 1978 the Canadian economy would be buried or come to an end. Obviously the official opposition has since seen some kind of light. Perhaps they feel some degree of responsibility in presenting themselves to the Canadian people as an opposition which finds the odd bright spot in a potentially very exciting economic picture. Presumably they have taken the pipeline project as something they should support.
This is indeed an historic bill. As has been stated previously, the Alaska Highway pipeline will involve some $10 billion in all, representing some 5,500 miles of pipeline construction. By way of simple comparison, this compares with the project some 20 years ago of TransCanada Pipelines. It involved a total expenditure at that time of something in the neighbourhood of $375 million, less than one tenth of this amount. There is no question that the project in this legislation is the most exciting project to face this nation and the private sector in North America for a very long time, and perhaps the largest ever.
The project has been overwhelmingly endorsed by the United States Congress. This is important. There is nothing to be ashamed of when the Canadian government can come to an agreement with the U.S. on a project of this magnitude which will mean so much to Canadians in terms of Canadian jobs in the immediate years to come. This is commendable. The fact that the U.S. Congress endorsed it overwhelmingly in the way they have is an indication of the type of united effort that can help make our joint economies tick.
The purpose of this bill is to establish an agency to ensure that this gigantic project is planned and implemented in a way that will maximize the industrial and social benefits for the Canadian people. From it Canada will be assured access to its own reserves in the Mackenzie delta in the long-term future by the only economic means currently available. We will have substantial assistance from the United States in building part of that link. It is obviously important to Canadians that we can and will preserve access to this important frontier area as we attempt to meet our long-term goal of energy self-reliance.
It is worth placing again on the record that implementation of the agreement with the United States is an important step in further strengthening our bonds with that country. There is no point in anyone on this continent pretending that he lives in a complete vacuum. Obviously it is important, where feasible and in our national interest, to undertake projects in joint partnership with our very large neighbour to the south.

Northern Pipeline
The pipeline will provide a boost to consumer and business confidence in both countries. The words of the Leader of the Opposition earlier this year indicated that he saw nothing on the horizon to provide any boost in confidence for Canadians. He knew this bill was coming. I guess he and his party did not have time to take a good look at it. Now that the bill is before the House the are supportive of it. We are glad they are. It is obviously something that is of substantial benefit to all Canadians. It is somewhat reassuring that the opposition see that now that the bill is before them. It is estimated that some
100,000	man-years of employment will be involved in this project. Eventually our international balance of payments will be improved. These are two areas of concern to thinking Canadians at this time.
There is another matter of concern. Preference will be given to Yukon residents in terms of training and hiring for construction work. In turn, this training and experience will enhance employment opportunities for the entire Yukon labour force. The federal government will have to move in the direction of settlement of claims as quickly as possible. When introducing the bill for second reading, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) clearly indicated that every effort will be made to arrive at a fair and just settlement of these claims. This will be done in as quick order as possible.
The establishment of this northern pipeline agency is very important and I wish to spend a few moments talking about some of the important aspects of it. First, I want to deal with the matter of a government guarantee. This has been said before, but it is worth repeating. It is surprising that the NDP is anxious to see us create a monopoly in pipeline construction.

speechtext: There is not one of them in the House.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs

speechtext:
Indeed, they are not all satisfied that we should be doing anything to create a really competitive situation. I have been with members of that party in committees at various times when we have been talking about matters involving business in general, small business or medium sized business, and they have always been most anxious to ensure there has been an adequate form of competition in the country. However, in this case they are speaking against the concept of competition. It must have taken some very deep thinking to arrive at that conclusion. I presume that only within their deepest research background are they able to satisfy themselves about this.
Canadian suppliers will have to sharpen their pencils. They may have to cut some costs to be competitive on this matter of pipeline bidding. That is the way it should be. We as a government would be extremely guilty if we did anything to put forward a project of this magnitude and told Canadian suppliers that they could have the business, with no need to worry about the costs; simply supply the pipe and the bills will be paid. That is no way to promote efficiency in the production sector.
The fact that we have ensured that the competitive aspect must be present before Canadian manufacturers can win these contracts is extremely important, and rather than blame the Deputy Prime Minister for not securing guarantees which would have locked us into a monopolistic situation he should be highly commended for declining to take what might have seemed an easy nationalistic route and for taking the action he did.
This having been said, I would point out that there is provision in the bill for the government to block contracts which fail to provide what is considered to be an adequate Canadian content. So there is an override. These contracts must come before the government which will then have an opportunity to examine them and satisfy itself that the concept of Canadian content is being adhered to, as the Foothills group has indicated it has every intention of so doing.
Another important point has to do with the cost of the agency. Many people are complaining about increases in government expenditures. The cost of the agency will be borne directly by the pipeline companies and, of course, will eventually be reflected in the price of gas to consumers in the U.S.
In addition, the monitoring agency will be able to review the manpower plan to ensure that it makes maximum use of Canadian labour in all phases of the project. It will also be examining the procurement proposals put forward by the companies to see that there are fair competitive opportunities for maximum Canadian participation. The agency will be overseeing the financial arrangements and will ensure that any plan which the companies may come up with provides for majority Canadian control and that the debt is not conditional upon approval by the lenders of construction of a lateral to the Mackenzie River delta. This is an extremely important point.
There will also be provision in the rules governing the agency for the minimization of legal delays which could be occasioned by various objections during the course of the project. I think it is important that, if we do intend to go ahead with this scheme, we should do so with the minimum of legal delays while at the same time ensuring fair play and a fair hearing to those who may object.
Hon. members have talked about the direct and indirect benefits which will be derived from the pipeline. I noticed today one item of incidental cost. Some $21 million is to be spent on a series of frost heave and pipe burst tests in areas of northern Alberta and Alaska. Although this is only incidental in terms of the total expenditure it is, nevertheless, a tremendous amount of money, because when such a sum is injected into the economy it does a tremendous amount by way of providing jobs. And this is only one small item which I have taken from the group of many such items.
Another question which has been asked is this: How much labour will be moving in from the south? Well, I have stated earlier that preference will be given to the hiring of people from the Yukon, and to ensure that this is the case, southern labour will be recruited through hiring halls located in the

Nations of the world must build their future co-operatively. The fact that we are co-operating with the United States in this project is nothing to be ashamed of. It is something we can be proud of provided we are doing it in the national interest, as I believe is the case in this instance.
Northern Pipeline
We have a great deal in common on this continent and no amount of breast beating will ever change that situation. Last spring, along with other members of the House, I was privileged to take part in inter-parliamentary group discussions with members of the United States Senate and House of Representatives in Victoria. At that time we gave consideration to some of these energy issues and I was impressed to see the degree of goodwill which existed among us, the eagerness to work together on projects of this nature.
We should bear in mind that in the future co-operation will take place not only between Canada and the United States but between North America and Europe. One had only to attend the World Energy Congress in Turkey last fall to have become aware that the energy issue is very much a global situation. The fact that we are involving ourselves so heavily with another country at this time is an indication on our part that we understand the global nature of our over-all energy problems. We must look to the future. The oil and gas question is only one of the areas which must be dealt with. Let us get it out of the way now so that we can turn our attention to the solution of other energy problems.
There is no question that we need oil and gas from our northern frontier. Those of us who are members of the national resources committee and who had the opportunity to visit the north two years ago were overawed by the tremendous potential which exists in that part of the country. In order to encourage people to take advantage of this potential a start on a major project must be made. And this is where the current northwest pipeline project is so important.
There are questions about nuclear energy with which we have to deal. In the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works we are discussing matters relating to nuclear waste and other related aspects, and we cannot spend all our time on oil and gas pipelines. However, this is still the first step in our policy of energy self-reliance, and for that reason I think it is important.
In conclusion, I would like to refer to some comments I made during the pipeline debate last August. At that time I indicated that there are three important things we should obtain from a pipeline arrangement. I spoke very much in favour of proceeding with this project. The first important point I made was that this project would have a positive effect on the Canadian economy. I think that has now been proved to be the case. We have the figures. We are now talking in terms of real dollars which are going to be spent. There is no question that there will be a tremendous impact on our economy.
My second point related to the opportunity we have to participate in this project along with our neighbour to the south. I felt it was important for us to endeavour to enter into a joint project if that could work to our mutual advantage, and particularly to the advantage of Canada. Obviously that will be the case, and the negotiations so ably carried on by the Deputy Prime Minister are indicative of that.

February 21, 1978
Northern Pipeline
The last thing I mentioned was that there is a need for us to do everything we can to stimulate investment in the north. We need the potential oil and gas reserves that are in our frontier areas, and a cancellation of the project would obviously have had a very negative effect on the potential for new investment to move in. The project will now go ahead, and I think the potential will be tremendous and will augur well for the possibility of finding additional reserves in the Mackenzie delta which in time may justify the type of pipeline that was earlier proposed but at this point is simply not feasible.
In summary, it is good to know that there is considerable support for this project coming from different parts of the House. There is a realization from time to time that parliamentarians of all parties must stop talking about all the things they perceive as not happening and start supporting some of the projects this government is putting in place that are indeed making things happen and making the economy tick. There is a clear realization that elected representatives should stand behind some of those projects and support them.

Mr. Speaker, in speaking in this debate and in dealing with the legislation concerning the Foothills pipeline project there are certain aspects of the bill which I would like to see strengthened. Although I support the bill in

principle, I certainly hope that by specifying those aspects which I want to see strengthened and by pointing out shortcomings in the bill I can thereby urge members of the special committee to incorporate certain changes in the bill at the committee stage or at later stages so that the bill can be unanimously supported.
The reason I am pleased to be taking part in this debate is that the whole matter of energy, energy supplies and especially energy conservation has been an ongoing concern which I have had for a long time. In addition, I am given this opportunity to look at certain problems of northern development and aboriginal rights which have been and are of ongoing interest and great concern to me. However, most importantly, at this time when the unity of this country is in question everywhere, this mammoth project which is shortly to be undertaken must be one which becomes a symbol of unity for all Canadians, a catalyst which will help pull us together and a monument to our shared interests whether we live east or west, north or south. It must not be allowed to become an element of tension or a divisive element between groups, whether racial or geographic, at this crucial time in our history. There is always the possibility that that can happen.
During this debate we have heard a great deal about steel, pipes, jobs and energy needs. We have heard what this project means in economic terms. All these things are important, but for a few minutes I would like to stand back and try to understand what this pipeline means to Canada as a country of the north.
As Mr. Justice Berger pointed out in the report of the Mackenzie Valley pipeline inquiry, "We look upon the north as our last frontier". He also said: "We think of ourselves as a northern people". It would not be an exaggeration to say that, to a great extent, the way in which the Canadian north is developed and the way in which this project in particular is developed will be a reflection of what we are as Canadians and what our values are. It is not an exaggeration to say that the pipeline and all the issues surrounding it are a reflection of what Canada is all about.
This project is about people. It is about native people, non-native northerners, Canadian entrepreneurs and interested southerners. It is about reconciling the various interests of all these groups of people. As such, it reflects the multicultural nature of this country as a whole. However, more than that, it reflects in a very real way the tension between the dominant interest group in this country and a special minority group, a tension which, in another form, presently exists between Quebec and the rest of the country. Our experience with that latter situation and the crisis that has developed in our confederation as a result should make us more sensitive to the needs and wishes of the native people of the north. We must not do anything at this point in our country's history that would add to the problems of national unity by further alienating a minority group of people who already have cause for resentment because of past injustices.
